examples.script:
Grandfather's Old Radio

When Sota helped his grandmother clean the storage room, he found a small brown radio with a silver handle. "That was your grandfather's favorite radio forty years ago," his grandmother said. Sota turned the switch, but no sound came out.

Sota liked learning how machines worked. He asked if he could take the radio to Mr. Yamada, a retired electrician who lived next door. Mr. Yamada smiled and opened the back cover carefully. Inside, one thin wire had come loose, and dust covered the speaker.

For an hour, Mr. Yamada showed Sota how to brush away the dust gently and reconnect the wire safely. When they put new batteries in and turned the dial, clear jazz music filled the room! Sota was amazed by the warm sound.

That evening, Sota placed the working radio on the kitchen table. When his grandmother heard an old song from her youth, tears came to her eyes, and she thanked Sota again and again.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 大問4 読解｜第1回（問26〜35）
examples.script:
A Useful Map

Last summer, Ren moved to a small town with his family. He did not know anyone there. He liked riding his bicycle, so he often went out to find new places. One afternoon, he found a beautiful pond behind the station. He wanted to tell his grandmother about it, but she did not know how to get there.

Ren decided to draw a map of the town. First, he visited the library to find an old map. It showed the streets, but it did not show the new park or the pond. Ren rode around town again and took notes. He also talked to people at the shops. They told him about a quiet garden and a small bakery.

Ren put these places on his map. He drew pictures and used large letters because his grandmother could not read small writing easily. When the map was finished, he took her to the pond. She found the way by looking at his map.

Later, a librarian saw Ren's map. She asked him to make copies for the library. Ren was surprised, but he was happy to help. Now new people in town can take a free map from the library. Ren has also made friends with some children who used his map.

examples.script:
The Vegetable Stamp Postcards

During summer vacation, twelve-year-old Riku helped his mother cook curry for lunch. When she sliced the green tops off two okra pods and cut the root base off a bunch of komatsuna greens, Riku noticed something surprising: the cut okra looked like a five-pointed star, and the komatsuna stem looked like a blooming rose!

"Wait—don't throw those scraps into the bin yet!" Riku said. Remembering an art project from elementary school, he dried the vegetable ends on a paper towel, dipped them lightly into watercolor paint on a sponge, and pressed them onto blank white postcards.

Green okra stars and pink komatsuna roses filled the cards in minutes. Riku added a short summer greeting—"How are you doing in the August heat?"—and mailed one card each to his grandparents in Toyama and his uncle in Kobe.

Three days later, his grandmother called laughing. She had framed Riku's postcard beside the kitchen calendar and tried stamping bell-pepper rings herself!

examples.script:
The Vegetable Stamp Bag

Hina's art class had an interesting project in October: each student received a plain white cloth tote bag and had to decorate it using natural shapes. At first, Hina thought about pressing autumn leaves onto the cloth, just like many of her classmates.

That evening, while helping her father make curry, Hina watched him cut off the bottom of a green okra pod and the root end of a lotus root. When she looked at the leftover pieces on the cutting board, she noticed something surprising. The cut okra looked like a neat five-pointed star, and the lotus root had a ring of pretty holes like a flower!

Hina asked her father if she could wash and dry those vegetable ends instead of throwing them away. The next day in art class, she dipped the okra and lotus root into fabric paint—yellow, green, and dark blue—and stamped patterns across her bag.

Her classmates gathered around her desk in amazement. Hina gave the finished bag to her father so he could carry vegetables home from the market every week.

examples.script:
A Useful Map

Last summer, Ren moved to a small town with his family. He did not know anyone there. He liked riding his bicycle, so he often went out to find new places. One afternoon, he found a beautiful pond behind the station. He wanted to tell his grandmother about it, but she did not know how to get there.

Ren decided to draw a map of the town. First, he visited the library to find an old map. It showed the streets, but it did not show the new park or the pond. Ren rode around town again and took notes. He also talked to people at the shops. They told him about a quiet garden and a small bakery.

Ren put these places on his map. He drew pictures and used large letters because his grandmother could not read small writing easily. When the map was finished, he took her to the pond. She found the way by looking at his map.

Later, a librarian saw Ren's map. She asked him to make copies for the library. Ren was surprised, but he was happy to help. Now new people in town can take a free map from the library. Ren has also made friends with some children who used his map.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 大問4 読解｜第2回（問26〜35）
examples.script:
A Box for Lost Gloves

Every winter, Mr. Oda, the school caretaker, found many gloves and scarves near the bicycle area. Students dropped them on windy mornings and did not notice. Mr. Oda put them in a box inside his small office, but few students came to ask for them.

One day, a seventh-grade student named Haru lost one blue glove. When he visited Mr. Oda's office, he saw dozens of lost items in the dark box. It took ten minutes to find his glove because everything was mixed together.

Haru had an idea. With Mr. Oda's permission, he and his art club friends painted a wooden board and put hooks on it. They hung the board in the main hallway, right beside the shoe lockers. Each hook had a label for the day of the week when an item was found.

The next week, students started checking the board every morning. Because they could see the items clearly on their way to class, almost all the gloves and scarves went back to their owners within a few days. Mr. Oda thanked Haru and gave the art club some warm cocoa.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 大問4 読解｜第3回（問26〜35）
examples.script:
Letters Across the Sea

Last autumn, Ms. Green's English class started a postcard exchange with a school in New Zealand. Each student got a partner. Hina's partner was a boy named Liam. In her first postcard, Hina wrote about her town's autumn festival and drew a small red lantern. However, she was worried that her English sentences were too short.

Three weeks later, postcards arrived from New Zealand. Liam loved Hina's drawing! He sent a postcard with a picture of sheep on a green hill. He wrote, "In New Zealand, October is spring, so baby lambs are everywhere now." Hina was surprised because the seasons were opposite.

For her second card, Hina wanted to share more. She went to the park, picked up two yellow ginkgo leaves, and taped one onto a card after pressing it flat in a thick dictionary. She wrote five sentences about how the trees changed color in November.

In December, Liam sent a photo of his class display board. Hina's yellow leaf was in the center, and many students wrote nice comments around it. Hina felt proud and decided to write longer letters next year.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 大問4 読解｜第13回（問26〜35）
examples.script:
Repairing Grandfather's Wooden Clock

On the wall of thirteen-year-old Shun's living room hung an old octagonal wooden clock that had belonged to his great-grandfather. Every hour, its brass pendulum used to chime softly, until one winter morning the hands stopped at ten-fifteen.

Shun's mother thought they would have to throw it away because modern battery shops didn't fix wind-up clocks. That Saturday, however, Shun spotted a tiny shop near the shotengai arcade with a hand-painted sign: "Takahashi Watch & Clock Repair."

Inside, seventy-five-year-old Mr. Takahashi opened the back panel with a small screwdriver and smiled. "Nothing is broken," he told Shun. "Old oil inside the gears simply dried up in the cold." Letting Shun watch through a magnifying glass, he cleaned each brass wheel with a soft brush and added two tiny drops of fresh clock oil.

When the warm chime rang out again at home that evening, Shun's grandfather clapped with joy—and Shun decided he wanted to learn how mechanical things work too.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 大問4 読解｜第15回（問26〜35）
examples.script:
The Bookshop Cat's Bookmark

Near fourteen-year-old Nanami's cram school stood an old secondhand bookshop called Kusunoki Books. Whenever Nanami had twenty minutes before her evening math class, she liked browsing its tall wooden shelves—especially because a plump orange cat named Kinako often napped on a cushion beside the cash register.

One rainy Tuesday, Nanami bought a mystery novel about a detective on a train. When the owner, Mrs. Hori, handed her the paper-wrapped book, she slipped a handmade bookmark inside. On it was a small rubber-stamp picture of Kinako wearing round glasses and reading!

"My granddaughter carved that eraser stamp for our shop's fiftieth anniversary this month," Mrs. Hori explained proudly. "There are four seasonal Kinako designs—spring cherry blossoms, summer watermelon, autumn acorns, and winter kotatsu."

Nanami loved the autumn acorn bookmark so much that she finished the mystery novel in four days—and brought her best friend Aoi to Kusunoki Books the very next week.

examples.script:
The Rainy-Day Board Games

At Aoba Junior High School, students loved playing soccer outside during lunch break. On rainy weeks in June, however, the schoolyard was closed. Many students sat quietly at their desks or crowded the hallways with nothing to do.

Kotaro, a member of the student council, talked with his classmates about this problem. He remembered that his grandfather had taught him shogi and simple card games on rainy afternoons. Kotaro asked teachers if the council could open one empty classroom on the first floor as a "Rainy-Day Game Room" during lunch.

The principal liked the idea, as long as students followed clear rules: games had to finish five minutes before afternoon classes, and everyone had to put all pieces back in their boxes. Teachers and families donated chess sets, reversi boards, and word-card games.

On the first rainy Tuesday, more than thirty students from different grades visited the room. Seventh graders played reversi against ninth graders and made new friends. Soon, some students even looked forward to rainy days!

examples.script:
Grandpa's Wooden Birdhouse

During spring break, twelve-year-old Mao stayed with her grandparents in Nagano for four days. Behind their house stood two tall apple trees. Every morning, Mao heard small wild birds singing in the branches, so she wanted to watch them more closely.

On the second day, her grandfather opened his small workshop and showed Mao some clean cedar boards left over from repairing a fence. "Why don't we build a birdhouse together?" he asked. He taught Mao how to measure the wood carefully with a metal ruler and smooth the edges with sandpaper.

Her grandfather made one important point: the round entrance hole had to be just three centimeters wide. If the hole was too big, crows might reach inside; if it was too small, even little chickadees could not enter. They hung the finished birdhouse on the lower branch of an apple tree and placed a dish of water nearby.

Before Mao went home on the fourth morning, a pair of small gray-and-white birds flew into the box carrying dry moss. Mao took a photo from the window and promised to visit again in summer.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 大問4 読解｜第11回（問26〜35）
examples.script:
Learning the Sign for "Delicious"

Every Wednesday afternoon, thirteen-year-old Ren stops at Hidamari Bakery near his junior high school to buy warm walnut rolls. Two months ago, a cheerful college student named Mr. Mori started working at the register. Small cards on the counter explained that Mr. Mori was deaf, so customers pointed to bread labels or held up fingers to show how many rolls they wanted.

Ren liked Mr. Mori's bright smile, yet he felt a little sad that he could only nod when leaving. That night, Ren borrowed an introductory Japanese Sign Language book with clear illustrations from the town library. He practiced three phrases in front of his mirror: "Hello," "Thank you," and "Last week's bread was delicious!"

The following Wednesday, after receiving his bag of walnut rolls, Ren tapped his right cheek lightly and touched his chin—the sign for "delicious"—followed by "thank you." Mr. Mori's eyes lit up with surprise. He signed back slowly, teaching Ren the sign for "bread."

Now Ren learns one new sign each week, and their thirty-second chat at the counter is his favorite part of Wednesday.

When Owen began helping at a small local museum, he learned the names of many old tools. He expected visitors to ask about them. examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第1回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第12回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
Bilingual Labels at the Town Museum

Fourteen-year-old Haruka loved visiting the small Folk Craft Museum in her castle town, which displayed wooden lanterns, indigo kimonos, and bamboo fishing baskets made a century ago. One Sunday in May, she saw two foreign tourists staring curiously at a woven bamboo fish trap. Because the display cards were written only in Japanese, the visitors left looking puzzled.

Haruka spoke with the museum director, Mr. Fujita, who admitted that his two-person staff was too busy to translate eighty display cards. The next day, Haruka proposed a summer volunteer project to her English club advisor, Ms. Carter.

Seven club members visited the museum with notebooks, asked Mr. Fujita how each tool had actually been used, and drafted short two-sentence explanations in simple English. Simply looking up dictionary words wasn't enough; Ms. Carter helped them explain cultural ideas—such as how river fish swam into the funnel shape but couldn't swim back out.

In September, QR codes and neat English cards stood beside thirty key exhibits, and Haruka felt thrilled watching overseas visitors nod with understanding.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第2回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
A Quiet Shelf at the Bakery

Maya's parents ran a small bakery near an elementary school. Every afternoon around three o'clock, parents and children stopped by to buy melon bread and rolls. While adults chose bread, young children often got bored and ran around the narrow shop. Maya worried that someone might bump into the hot trays.

One rainy Saturday, Maya was cleaning her bookshelf at home. She found about thirty picture books that she had loved when she was little. They were still in clean condition. Instead of selling them, Maya asked her father if she could put a low wooden crate in one corner of the bakery.

Her father agreed, so Maya placed a soft mat and the picture books in the corner. She also wrote a small sign: "Read one here, or borrow it until your next visit!" On Monday afternoon, two little boys sat on the mat right away and looked at a book about trains while their mother shopped.

Soon, something unexpected happened. Neighborhood customers began bringing their own children's old picture books to add to the crate. Some older students even left short sticky notes inside the covers recommending their favorite pages. The shop became safer and calmer, and families started visiting more often just to return a book and buy fresh bread.

examples.script:
Preparing for the Debate Match

From: Kaito
To: Sara
Subject: Saturday's practice match

Hi Sara,
Good job at English club today! Our practice debate with West Junior High School is getting close. Their teacher just emailed Ms. Ito: one of their members caught a cold, so we will meet online by video call instead of going to their school this Saturday.

We can use the computer room on the third floor of our school. Let's meet there at 9:30 a.m. to test the microphone before the match starts at 10:00 a.m.

Could you print three copies of our note cards tomorrow? The printer at my house ran out of black ink tonight. I will bring the timer and the topic list.

See you tomorrow,
Kaito

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第3回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
Learning the Bus Routes

When Leo started junior high school, he began taking the city bus for the first time. On his third morning, he got on a bus with the same orange stripe as usual, without reading the sign on the front. Twenty minutes later, the bus turned toward the port instead of his school! A kind driver told him how to transfer back, and Leo arrived just before the bell.

That evening, Leo looked at the city bus map online, but the lines overlapped like colorful spaghetti. His younger sister, Mio, who would enter the same school next year, said she was scared of making the same mistake.

Leo decided to make a simple pocket guide for students. Over two weekends, he rode four main routes from the central terminal, counting how many stops each took to reach the school, the library, and the sports park. He noticed that bus numbers ending in 2 always went east toward his school, while numbers ending in 5 went west toward the port.

He folded a single sheet of thick paper into a card that fit inside a student ID case. On one side, he drew the three main landmarks and wrote the number rule in bold letters. When Leo showed the card to his homeroom teacher, the school printed copies for all new seventh graders the following April. Mio carried hers proudly on her very first day.

From: Haruka, Editor-in-Chief
To: School Newspaper Club Members
Subject: Interview with the cafeteria nutritionist

Hi everyone,
Good news! Ms. Kimura, our school nutritionist, agreed to give us an interview for the winter issue of our school newspaper. She will tell us how she plans warm soup menus using vegetables grown in our city.

Originally, we hoped to meet her this Wednesday after school, but she has a city meeting that afternoon. Instead, we will interview her on Friday from 4:00 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. in the home economics room.

Two members—Sota and Mei—will ask the questions, and Yuna will take photos. Could everyone else write one question you want to ask Ms. Kimura and put it in our club box by Thursday noon?

Thanks,
Haruka

examples.script:
Growing Herbs by the Cafeteria

Behind Minami Junior High School's cafeteria lay a narrow strip of dry ground where nothing grew except weeds. Whenever students lined up for lunch, they looked out the hallway window at that bare space. Shun, who belonged to the gardening club, wondered if the club could turn it into something useful.

Instead of planting ordinary flowers, Shun suggested growing kitchen herbs such as parsley, rosemary, and mint. He spoke with Mr. Ono, the head cook of the school cafeteria. Mr. Ono loved the idea, explaining that fresh herbs were often too expensive to buy in large amounts for school lunches, even though a small pinch made tomato soup and roasted potatoes smell wonderful.

In April, six club members pulled out the weeds, mixed compost into the soil, and planted herb seedlings. Because the cafeteria roof blocked some rain, the students took turns watering the bed every morning before homeroom. Mr. Ono also taught them which leaves to trim so the plants would grow thicker.

By June, the herb bed was bright green and fragrant. The cafeteria served "Garden Herb Potato Soup," and a small card by the lunch counter thanked the gardening club. Seeing classmates enjoy the aroma made every early morning worthwhile for Shun and his friends.

examples.script:
The Repair Bench at the Shopping Street

For years, an empty shuttered shop stood in the middle of Suzuran Shopping Street in fifteen-year-old Kaito's neighborhood. Fewer people walked past it each month, and neighboring grocers worried the whole arcade was losing its energy.

In April, Kaito's retired grandfather, a former high school woodworking teacher, rented the small space with two old friends—an electrician and a seamstress—and opened "Saturday Fix-It Corner." Every Saturday afternoon, residents brought wobbly dining chairs, quiet transistor radios, or schoolbags with broken zippers. Instead of simply dropping items off, owners sat beside the volunteers and learned how to tighten a loose joint or sew on a sturdy patch themselves.

Kaito began helping at the reception desk twice a month, greeting visitors and writing repair tags. One afternoon, an elementary school boy beamed with pride after gluing his favorite wooden toy train back together with Kaito's grandfather.

Soon, people waiting their turn bought croquettes and green tea from nearby shops, bringing lively conversation back to the once-quiet street.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第14回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
The Lunchtime Weather Broadcast

When fourteen-year-old Shun joined the broadcasting committee at Aoba Junior High School, his Tuesday job was reading a two-minute weather forecast during lunch. At first, Shun simply copied numbers from a weather website—"Sunny tomorrow, high of twenty-six degrees, twenty percent chance of rain"—and noticed that nobody in the classrooms really listened.

One rainy afternoon, the baseball captain complained that players never knew whether the clay infield would dry in time for after-school practice. That gave Shun an idea. With advice from his science teacher, Mr. Hori, Shun began checking wind speed and morning humidity on the school's rooftop weather sensor and translating raw numbers into practical school tips.

Instead of dry figures, Tuesday broadcasts sounded lively: "Strong west breeze this afternoon—the tennis courts should dry by three-thirty, and bicyclists riding east will have a tailwind home!" Art club members painting outdoors and students hanging laundry at home soon started tuning in eagerly.

By autumn, three seventh graders asked to join the committee after hearing Shun's broadcasts, teaching him that useful information begins with imagining the listener's day.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第15回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
The Left-Handed Can Opener

Fifteen-year-old Soma was the only left-handed person in his family. Most days he barely thought about it, though using classroom scissors or pouring soup from ladles with spouts on only one side always felt awkward.

During a home economics cooking test in October, each student had to open a tin of sweet corn within two minutes. As right-handed classmates twisted standard crank-style openers effortlessly, Soma struggled: holding the handle in his left hand forced the cutting wheel outward, slipping off the metal rim again and again.

Seeing Soma's frustration, his home economics teacher, Ms. Ide, didn't deduct points. Instead, she brought three kitchen tools to the next class—a butterfly opener that worked from either side, ambidextrous kitchen shears, and a ladle with spouts on both sides—and asked right-handed students to try opening a paper cup using their non-dominant left hand.

Gasps of "That's so tricky!" echoed around the room. Experiencing that small hurdle firsthand got the whole class noticing universal design on station ticket gates, shampoo bottles, and rulers all week.

examples.script:
The Sound Map of Sakura Town

In social studies class, Mr. Endo asked his eighth-grade students to research something special about Sakura Town. Most groups chose famous historical buildings or local sweets, but Riku's group wanted to try a fresh topic. While waiting at a railroad crossing after school, Riku heard the evening chimes from the town hall, frogs in the rice fields, and the bell of a tofu seller's cart.

"What if we make a map of sounds that belong to our town?" Riku suggested. His three teammates loved the idea. Over two weeks, they walked through six neighborhoods with a small voice recorder and notebooks. Before recording inside shops, they politely explained their school project and asked permission.

They collected eighteen distinct sounds, including the rhythmic clack of a weaving loom, seagulls at the fishing port, and steam rising from a hot-spring footbath. On a large poster map, they drew colored icons for each place and wrote what time of day the sound could be heard.

At the school presentation day, visitors scanned codes beside the map to listen through headphones. Several elderly residents smiled and said the sounds reminded them how lively their everyday town really was.

examples.script:
The Hand-Drawn Evacuation Map

In September, fourteen-year-old Nanami's social studies class walked around their neighborhood to check disaster safety signs. Nanami's group visited the riverside block near the shopping street, where many elderly residents lived. Although a metal map at the station showed the route to Midori Elementary School—the local evacuation shelter—Nanami noticed a problem when she actually walked the route.

One narrow lane on the official map went down ten steep stone steps, making it impossible for wheelchairs or baby strollers to pass. Even worse, tall hedges hid a small wooden sign at the corner.

Nanami's group walked every side street for an hour and found a slightly longer but completely flat path past the post office. Back at school, they drew a large, colorful map with big letters, photos of landmarks like the red mailbox, and walking times measured at a slow pace.

When the neighborhood association laminated their map and posted it outside the supermarket, several older shoppers thanked the students for noticing what hurried commuters had missed.

examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第7回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
The Secondhand Textbook Shelf

When Airi entered ninth grade, her older cousin gave her two English workbooks and an atlas of historical maps that he no longer needed. Although a few margin notes were written neatly in pencil, the books were clean and helpful—especially the colored maps, which Airi used every evening at home while leaving her own heavy school atlas in her locker.

Airi wondered how many useful study guides and reference books were thrown away every March when ninth graders graduated. She talked with Ms. Honda, the teacher in charge of the student council, and proposed setting up a "Pass-It-On Study Shelf" inside the career guidance room during March.

Graduating students were invited to donate clean reference books, vocabulary cards, and geometry tool sets, along with a sticky note offering one piece of study advice to younger students. Over a hundred items were collected in just four days.

When seventh and eighth graders came to choose books in April, the sticky notes proved just as popular as the books themselves. Reading encouraging messages from seniors who had sat at the same desks gave younger students fresh motivation for the new term.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第12回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
Bilingual Labels at the Town Museum

Fourteen-year-old Haruka loved visiting the small Folk Craft Museum in her castle town, which displayed wooden lanterns, indigo kimonos, and bamboo fishing baskets made a century ago. One Sunday in May, she saw two foreign tourists staring curiously at a woven bamboo fish trap. Because the display cards were written only in Japanese, the visitors left looking puzzled.

Haruka spoke with the museum director, Mr. Fujita, who admitted that his two-person staff was too busy to translate eighty display cards. The next day, Haruka proposed a summer volunteer project to her English club advisor, Ms. Carter.

Seven club members visited the museum with notebooks, asked Mr. Fujita how each tool had actually been used, and drafted short two-sentence explanations in simple English. Simply looking up dictionary words wasn't enough; Ms. Carter helped them explain cultural ideas—such as how river fish swam into the funnel shape but couldn't swim back out.

In September, QR codes and neat English cards stood beside thirty key exhibits, and Haruka felt thrilled watching overseas visitors nod with understanding.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第14回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
The Lunchtime Weather Broadcast

When fourteen-year-old Shun joined the broadcasting committee at Aoba Junior High School, his Tuesday job was reading a two-minute weather forecast during lunch. At first, Shun simply copied numbers from a weather website—"Sunny tomorrow, high of twenty-six degrees, twenty percent chance of rain"—and noticed that nobody in the classrooms really listened.

One rainy afternoon, the baseball captain complained that players never knew whether the clay infield would dry in time for after-school practice. That gave Shun an idea. With advice from his science teacher, Mr. Hori, Shun began checking wind speed and morning humidity on the school's rooftop weather sensor and translating raw numbers into practical school tips.

Instead of dry figures, Tuesday broadcasts sounded lively: "Strong west breeze this afternoon—the tennis courts should dry by three-thirty, and bicyclists riding east will have a tailwind home!" Art club members painting outdoors and students hanging laundry at home soon started tuning in eagerly.

By autumn, three seventh graders asked to join the committee after hearing Shun's broadcasts, teaching him that useful information begins with imagining the listener's day.

examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

examples.script:
A visitor’s question

When Owen began helping at a small local museum, he learned the names of many old tools. He expected visitors to ask about them. Instead, several children asked how people used the tools in daily life. Owen could name each tool but could not explain its use clearly. The next week, he asked an older volunteer to show him. Together they made short demonstration videos. Now Owen plays these videos during his tours. He still introduces the names, but he spends more time showing what the tools actually did.

Summer break starts next week, and the music room will be painted from July 22 to July 26. Because of this work, we cannot practice in the music room during those five days. Instead, we will use Room 104 on the first floor.

Also, our new sheet music for the autumn festival arrived this morning. Come and pick up your copy after classes today.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第7回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
The Secondhand Textbook Shelf

When Airi entered ninth grade, her older cousin gave her two English workbooks and an atlas of historical maps that he no longer needed. Although a few margin notes were written neatly in pencil, the books were clean and helpful—especially the colored maps, which Airi used every evening at home while leaving her own heavy school atlas in her locker.

Airi wondered how many useful study guides and reference books were thrown away every March when ninth graders graduated. She talked with Ms. Honda, the teacher in charge of the student council, and proposed setting up a "Pass-It-On Study Shelf" inside the career guidance room during March.

Graduating students were invited to donate clean reference books, vocabulary cards, and geometry tool sets, along with a sticky note offering one piece of study advice to younger students. Over a hundred items were collected in just four days.

When seventh and eighth graders came to choose books in April, the sticky notes proved just as popular as the books themselves. Reading encouraging messages from seniors who had sat at the same desks gave younger students fresh motivation for the new term.

Preparing for Kindergarten Visit

From: Ms. Aoki, Home Economics Teacher
To: Class 3-B Students
Subject: Picture-card theater at Himawari Kindergarten

Dear Class 3-B,
Next Tuesday morning, our class will walk to Himawari Kindergarten to perform our handmade picture-card stories (kamishibai) for the five-year-old children. You have all drawn colorful, expressive pictures!

During Friday's class, please practice reading your script aloud slowly and clearly. Five-year-olds understand the story much better when you pause for two seconds before sliding each card. Also, check that no staples or sharp tape corners stick out from the edges of your cardboard frames.

On Tuesday, bring clean indoor shoes in a bag and avoid wearing rings, pins, or long necklaces so nothing catches on the children's clothes while playing games afterward.

Ms. Aoki

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第9回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
Learning Braille on Everyday Boxes

One rainy Saturday, fifteen-year-old Mei went to a convenience store to buy shampoo for her family. At home in the bathroom, her mother pointed to a row of tiny raised lines on the side of the shampoo bottle, while the conditioner bottle next to it was smooth. "Do you know why only the shampoo has those bumps?" her mother asked. "So people can tell them apart with their eyes closed—and it helps people with visual impairments, too."

Once Mei noticed that design, she began spotting raised dots—Braille—all around town: on elevator buttons, station handrails, canned drinks, and town office maps. Curious to understand what the dots actually spelled, she borrowed a beginner's Braille chart from the city library.

At first, reading with her fingertips felt impossible; all the dots seemed to blur together. After two weeks of practicing ten minutes each night, however, she could read floor numbers and "push/pull" door signs.

During her school's welfare study week, Mei brought empty household bottles and station photos to class. Letting classmates close their eyes and touch the bottles helped everyone realize how thoughtful small designs make daily life easier for all.

examples.script:
Growing Loofah Curtains at School

Last summer, the third-floor classrooms facing south at Nishi Junior High School became uncomfortably warm every afternoon, even with electric fans running. During an environment committee meeting in April this year, fifteen-year-old Mei suggested planting "green curtains" of climbing loofah vines outside the first-floor science room first as a test.

With advice from Mr. Oka, the school caretaker, twelve committee members dug compost into long planter boxes, stretched netting up to the second-floor balcony, and sowed loofah seeds in early May. Taking turns watering the boxes before homeroom became their daily habit—even during rainy weeks when weeds popped up.

By late July, broad green leaves covered the entire net and bright yellow flowers bloomed. Thermometers placed by the science club showed that the windowsill behind the loofah leaves was four degrees cooler than an unshaded window next door!

In October, the students dried the mature loofah gourds and cut them into natural dish sponges for the cooking room, proud that one packet of seeds had cooled their school and left zero waste.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 大問3 読解｜第15回（問21〜30）
examples.script:
The Left-Handed Can Opener

Fifteen-year-old Soma was the only left-handed person in his family. Most days he barely thought about it, though using classroom scissors or pouring soup from ladles with spouts on only one side always felt awkward.

During a home economics cooking test in October, each student had to open a tin of sweet corn within two minutes. As right-handed classmates twisted standard crank-style openers effortlessly, Soma struggled: holding the handle in his left hand forced the cutting wheel outward, slipping off the metal rim again and again.

Seeing Soma's frustration, his home economics teacher, Ms. Ide, didn't deduct points. Instead, she brought three kitchen tools to the next class—a butterfly opener that worked from either side, ambidextrous kitchen shears, and a ladle with spouts on both sides—and asked right-handed students to try opening a paper cup using their non-dominant left hand.

Gasps of "That's so tricky!" echoed around the room. Experiencing that small hurdle firsthand got the whole class noticing universal design on station ticket gates, shampoo bottles, and rulers all week.

examples.script:
Learning the Bus Routes

When Leo started junior high school, he began taking the city bus for the first time. On his third morning, he got on a bus with the same orange stripe as usual, without reading the sign on the front. Twenty minutes later, the bus turned toward the port instead of his school! A kind driver told him how to transfer back, and Leo arrived just before the bell.

That evening, Leo looked at the city bus map online, but the lines overlapped like colorful spaghetti. His younger sister, Mio, who would enter the same school next year, said she was scared of making the same mistake.

Leo decided to make a simple pocket guide for students. Over two weekends, he rode four main routes from the central terminal, counting how many stops each took to reach the school, the library, and the sports park. He noticed that bus numbers ending in 2 always went east toward his school, while numbers ending in 5 went west toward the port.

He folded a single sheet of thick paper into a card that fit inside a student ID case. On one side, he drew the three main landmarks and wrote the number rule in bold letters. When Leo showed the card to his homeroom teacher, the school printed copies for all new seventh graders the following April. Mio carried hers proudly on her very first day.

Subject: Binoculars and bird checklist for your forest trip!

Dear Rina,
Your dad mentioned that your eighth-grade class is going to Mount Akagi for nature observation next Wednesday! You're very welcome to use my lightweight birdwatching binoculars.

When you spot a bird in a tree, don't lift the binoculars right away—keep your eyes fixed on the branch first, and bring the eyepieces up to your eyes without looking down! That little trick makes finding small birds ten times easier.

Come over on Sunday afternoon so we can adjust the neck strap to fit you, and stay for your grandma's strawberry shortcake!

Love,
Grandpa

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問3 長文の語句空所補充｜第8回（問21〜22）
examples.script:
Why Stadium Grass Needs Artificial Sunlight

Modern soccer stadiums are built with steep, covered stands that shelter tens of thousands of fans from rain and wind, while keeping cheers echoing loudly around the pitch. For the groundskeepers tending the natural grass field, however, those towering roofs create a stubborn problem: even at noon on a sunny day, large sections of turf remain in deep shadow.

Grass blades need sunlight for photosynthesis, especially in winter when matches tear up wet soil and natural daylight hours are short. Without enough light, shaded goal areas quickly turn muddy and bare. To keep the turf thick and safe for players' ankles, many stadiums wheel out wide aluminum rigs fitted with high-efficiency grow lamps between matches. Sensors in the soil measure temperature and moisture so lamps warm and illuminate only the weakest patches. This targeted care (21).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第7回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Mist Vegetables Gently—and Leave Others Dry

Shoppers reaching for lettuce or broccoli in the produce aisle often hear a soft rumble of thunder from hidden speakers just before fine water droplets drift over the greens. Although the sound effect is playful, the misting system itself serves a practical purpose grounded in plant biology.

Even after harvest, leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, and parsley continue losing moisture through microscopic pores on their leaves. Because these greens have a large surface area and very thin outer skins, dry store air can leave them limp within hours, forcing grocers to throw away otherwise nutritious food. Periodic bursts of cool mist keep humidity high around the leaves and slow down wilting, while the brief sound warning lets customers step back so their sleeves stay dry.

Not every vegetable benefits from a shower, however. Onions, garlic, potatoes, and winter squash are stored in dry bins far from the mist nozzles. Evolved as underground bulbs or thick-skinned storage organs, these crops naturally resist drying out; getting them wet in a warm store actually encourages mold and premature sprouting. Tomatoes and mushrooms likewise spoil faster when damp.

In recent years, several grocery chains have replaced open misting with ultrasonic humidifiers that create fog droplets too tiny to wet surfaces. Because excess water no longer pools at the bottom of display trays, stores report less bacterial rot and longer shelf life.

Knowing how different vegetables respond to moisture helps shoppers at home too: leafy greens stay crisp wrapped in a slightly damp cloth in the fridge, whereas onions belong in a cool, dry basket.

Why Bakery Windows Fog Up Less Than Before

On cold winter mornings, small bakeries face a practical display problem. Warm steam rising from fresh trays of bread meets the icy glass of the front window and turns into tiny water droplets. While a misty window looks cozy in picture books, shop owners dislike it when passersby cannot see which breads have just come out of the oven.

Turning up the heater near the glass dries the window, yet dry hot air also makes uncovered croissants and crusty loaves lose moisture faster. A baker in Matsumoto found a simpler fix after talking with a neighbor who repaired eyeglasses. By installing a quiet ceiling fan that kept air moving gently across the glass and leaving a two-centimeter vent open near the top frame, the shop prevented warm damp air from sitting still against the cold pane. This adjustment (21) without drying out the bread.

Keeping the window clear had a welcome effect on morning sales. Commuters walking to the station could spot steaming walnut rolls from across the street and step inside on impulse. Sometimes solving an everyday shop problem requires (22) rather than buying a bigger heater.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問3 長文の語句空所補充｜第7回（問21〜22）
examples.script:
Why Libraries Lend Sewing Machines and Tools

For generations, people thought of public libraries solely as quiet halls lined with books, magazines, and newspapers. Over the past decade, however, dozens of municipal libraries have added an unexpected shelf near the checkout counter—one stocked with sewing machines, pruning shears, air-quality monitors, and cake pans.

The idea behind a "library of things" is straightforward. Many household tools are genuinely useful twice a year, yet sit gathering dust in a closet for the other fifty weeks. Buying a decent sewing machine just to hem two pairs of curtains is expensive, especially for students or young families living in compact apartments with little storage space. Borrowing equipment with an ordinary library card lets residents (21).

Sharing infrequent tools brings community benefits as well. Librarians often pair popular items with beginner workshops led by retired tailors or carpenters, turning solitary repairs into friendly learning sessions. In this way, lending practical tools extends a library's traditional mission: giving everyone equal access to (22) regardless of income.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問3 長文の語句空所補充｜第15回（問21〜22）
examples.script:
Why Manhole Covers Are Almost Always Round

Walk down almost any city street in the world, and the heavy cast-iron plates covering underground sewer and utility shafts share one unmistakable shape: they are round. Meanwhile, sidewalk grates for rainwater, subway ventilation panels, and telecom curb boxes are often rectangular. That contrast is no accident of tradition—civil engineers settled on circular manhole covers for hard-headed safety and practical reasons.

Consider what happens when workers lift a fifty-kilogram rectangular lid to climb down a ladder. Turned diagonally, a rectangle is narrower across its short side than across its corner-to-corner diagonal, meaning a careless slip could send the heavy iron plate plunging edge-first onto a technician below. A circle, by contrast, has the exact same diameter at every angle; resting on a slightly narrower circular lip inside the frame, a round cover physically (21).

Round lids simplify manufacturing and street work too. Foundries can turn circular rims smoothly on a lathe, workers never have to rotate a heavy cover to match corners when putting it back, and one worker can roll a round plate on its edge like a wheel instead of straining their back. Geometry here quietly protects (22).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第2回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
Why Old Roof Tiles Get a Second Job

Walk through an older Japanese town after a renovation project, and you may see stacks of dark gray clay roof tiles waiting beside a garden wall. Historically, clay tiles were prized because they protected wooden houses from heavy rain and summer heat for decades. Yet when old houses are replaced with modern buildings, thousands of still-solid tiles are removed every year. Disposing of them in landfills takes up space and wastes durable material.

In several regions, landscape designers and town workers have found practical ways to reuse discarded tiles without melting them down. Crushed into small pieces, the baked clay absorbs rainwater and releases it slowly, making it an ideal surface for park paths and tree beds. Unlike dark asphalt, crushed tile paths stay cooler under strong summer sun and allow weeds to be pulled out easily.

Whole tiles are useful as well. Placed upright in rows half-buried in soil, their gentle curves form neat borders around vegetable patches and flower beds. Some community gardens even stack tiles with narrow gaps between them to create cool shelters for frogs and helpful insects that eat garden pests.

Reusing tiles is not completely effortless. Workers must first remove nails, mortar, and cracked pieces with sharp edges so that paths and borders are safe to walk near. Even with this extra sorting step, local towns have found that cleaning and crushing old tiles nearby requires far less energy than manufacturing new concrete blocks and transporting them from distant factories.

For many residents, the greatest benefit is visual as well as environmental. Seeing familiar gray tiles along a new park walkway preserves a quiet connection to the town's past, turning construction waste into part of the neighborhood's character.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第5回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
Why Public Clocks Still Matter in the Smartphone Era

Almost everyone walking through a train station plaza or town square today carries an exact atomic-synced clock in a coat pocket. At first glance, spending municipal money to maintain large analog clocks on towers, schools, and park posts might seem outdated. Yet when cities remove broken public clocks instead of repairing them, residents surprisingly often petition to bring them back.

One reason is practical convenience in moments when hands are occupied. A parent holding a toddler's hand, a cyclist waiting at an intersection, or a commuter carrying grocery bags in winter gloves can check a clock face in half a second without unzipping a pocket. Even more importantly, pulling out a smartphone just to check the time frequently leads to unintended distraction—one glance at a notification banner, and five minutes vanish.

Urban designers point to a subtler social role as well. Unlike a private screen, a public clock creates a shared reference point in physical space. Saying "Let's meet under the station clock at two" gives friends and visitors an unmistakable landmark visible from across a crowded square. During major power or cellular outages following storms, wind-up or battery-backed tower clocks have also continued marking time calmly when digital displays went dark.

Maintaining outdoor clocks does require skilled hands. Gears exposed to freezing rain, sea breeze, and nesting birds must be cleaned and lubricated regularly, and fewer young technicians train in turret clockwork today. To keep costs manageable, some towns pair modern solar-charged movements behind historic dial faces, preserving the familiar look while simplifying upkeep.

Far from being mere nostalgia, a well-placed town clock quietly supports punctual, unhurried movement through shared streets.

examples.script:
Why Old Bridges Were Built with Roofs

Travel through rural valleys in Switzerland, Austria, North America, or parts of Japan, and you may cross a wooden bridge that looks remarkably like a long narrow barn floating above a river. Tourists often assume the roof and side walls were added so travelers and horses could stay dry during sudden storms—or so nervous farm animals would not fear the rushing water below.

While shelter was a pleasant bonus, carpenters of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries had a much more practical structural reason: protecting the heavy timber trusses underneath from rot. An uncovered wooden bridge exposed to rain, snow, and summer sun typically needed major replacement within fifteen to twenty years. Water seeped into joints where beams met, froze and expanded in winter, and invited wood-eating fungi.

Adding a lightweight roof and shingle siding cost extra lumber at the start, yet shielded the load-bearing beams from moisture. When minor roof shingles wore out, villagers could replace them cheaply without closing the bridge or rebuilding its main frame. Protected this way, many covered timber bridges lasted eighty to over a hundred years—four or five times longer than open wooden spans.

When affordable steel and reinforced concrete arrived in the twentieth century, engineers no longer needed roofs to weatherproof bridges. Nevertheless, communities that preserved historic covered bridges have gained unexpected value: calm pedestrian crossings, local landmarks, and living lessons in resource-saving craftsmanship.

Sometimes the smartest way to make a structure endure is not choosing a rarer material, but keeping everyday weather off its bones.

examples.script:
The quiet label

A small theatre once put a "quiet performance" label on certain shows. Staff expected it to welcome people who disliked sudden noise. However, a visitor explained that the label was unclear: did it mean the audience had to remain completely silent, or that the sound from the stage would be softer? The theatre asked several visitors to review its website. It then replaced the short label with a description of what would be different. These performances now use lower sound levels and leave a few lights on. Visitors may step outside and return. The theatre still offers ordinary performances, but it no longer expects a single label to explain every change.

examples.script:
Audio Descriptions at Live Theater

Going to see a live play is exciting partly because so much happens without words: an actor glances nervously at a clock, a door slowly opens at the back of the stage, or warm yellow light shifts to cold blue. For theatergoers who are blind or have low vision, however, these silent visual moments can make a story hard to follow if they rely on dialogue alone.

To bridge this gap, more theaters now offer "audio-described" performances. Audience members who request the service wear a lightweight earpiece connected to a small receiver. Sitting in a soundproof booth at the back of the hall, a trained describer watches the stage and speaks quietly into a microphone, slipping short phrases about costumes, facial expressions, and movements into the natural pauses between actors' lines.

Writing good audio description is more delicate than simply listing everything on stage. If a mystery character hides a key in a coat pocket, naming the key too early could spoil a surprise that sighted audience members discover only later. Conversely, saying too little leaves listeners confused when everyone else gasps or laughs. Describers therefore attend rehearsals in advance, consult directors, and time every sentence down to the second.

Some theaters have also introduced "touch tours" thirty minutes before the curtain rises. Visitors who use audio description are invited onto the stage to feel the texture of a velvet cape, examine a wooden prop sword, and walk across the set to understand the distance between rooms. When the play begins, a brief phrase like "she crosses to the oak table" immediately calls up a clear mental picture.

Actors and directors say preparing for these performances often sharpens their own craft as well. Explaining why a gesture or lighting change matters forces the creative team to think carefully about every visual choice on stage.

We will enter through the backstage door on the west side at 1:15 p.m.; the front glass doors will stay locked because no audience is attending. Warm-up exercises begin at 1:30 p.m., and recording runs from 2:15 p.m. to 3:45 p.m.

Cold winter air dries vocal cords quickly, so bring a bottle of plain room-temperature water. Please avoid milk tea or sweet juice right before singing, as sugar and dairy can coat your throat and make clear high notes harder. Cough drops may be used during breaks, not while standing on the risers.

Let's enjoy making a recording we'll remember!
Mr. Shinohara

Why Stadium Grass Needs Artificial Sunlight

Modern soccer stadiums are built with steep, covered stands that shelter tens of thousands of fans from rain and wind, while keeping cheers echoing loudly around the pitch. For the groundskeepers tending the natural grass field, however, those towering roofs create a stubborn problem: even at noon on a sunny day, large sections of turf remain in deep shadow.

Grass blades need sunlight for photosynthesis, especially in winter when matches tear up wet soil and natural daylight hours are short. Without enough light, shaded goal areas quickly turn muddy and bare. To keep the turf thick and safe for players' ankles, many stadiums wheel out wide aluminum rigs fitted with high-efficiency grow lamps between matches. Sensors in the soil measure temperature and moisture so lamps warm and illuminate only the weakest patches. This targeted care (21).

Although running grow rigs uses electricity, keeping natural turf healthy avoids costly mid-season resodding, where entire truckloads of grass must be stripped and replaced. Healthy roots hold the ground together, proving that great stadium architecture must consider (22) as carefully as spectator comfort.

Why Coastal Towns Paint Lighthouses in Distinct Stripes

Postcards of seacoasts often show a tall white lighthouse standing on a rocky headland. Travel along an actual coastline, however, and you quickly notice that neighboring lighthouses rarely look identical: one wears bold red-and-white horizontal bands, another spirals like a black-and-white barber pole, and a third is painted solid yellow.

At night, sailors identify lighthouses by their unique flash rhythm—for instance, two quick flashes every ten seconds. During daylight hours, however, a flashing lamp is hard to spot against bright sky or sea glare. Before satellite navigation existed, captains steering along a foggy coast with binoculars needed an unmistakable visual daytime marker, known to mariners as a "daymark." Giving adjacent towers contrasting patterns ensured that (21).

Background scenery also guides color choice. A pure white tower stands out sharply against dark pine forests, yet vanishes against chalk cliffs or winter snowdrifts, where red bands remain vivid. Even today, when ships carry digital chart plotters, maritime authorities maintain these painted daymarks as (22) whenever electronics fail at sea.

Why Wooden Cutting Boards Stay Popular in Professional Kitchens

When smooth plastic cutting boards entered home kitchens decades ago, many cooks assumed traditional wooden boards would soon disappear. Plastic boards were light, inexpensive, and easy to load into hot dishwashers. Yet walk into bakeries, sushi counters, and restaurant prep rooms today, and thick end-grain boards made of hinoki cypress, maple, or ginkgo wood remain a chef's favorite surface.

Knife care is the first reason cooks stay loyal to wood. Hard glass, stone, or stiff plastic dulls a finely sharpened steel edge quickly because the blade slams into an unyielding surface on every chop. Wood fibers, particularly when arranged vertically like bristles on a brush, part slightly under the knife edge and spring back afterward. This gentle cushion lets chefs (21).

Food-safety experiments also surprised early skeptics. Deep knife grooves in old plastic boards can trap moisture and bacteria even after a quick wash, whereas dry natural wood pulls liquid droplets inward via capillary action, leaving surface microbes without the water they need to multiply. Provided cooks wash a wooden board promptly and stand it upright to dry, traditional timber offers (22).

examples.script:
How Pocket Parks Cool Busy Neighborhoods

When city governments talk about expanding green space, residents often picture sprawling central parks with boating ponds and long jogging loops. Finding ten empty hectares inside an already crowded district, however, is nearly impossible. Instead, urban planners from Tokyo to Madrid are turning tiny leftover plots—a vacant corner lot, a former gas station, or two unused parking spaces—into "pocket parks."

Measuring smaller than a tennis court, a single pocket park may hold just four shade trees, a permeable brick path, a drinking fountain, and three wooden benches. Modest as that sounds, grouping dozens of small green oases a five-minute walk apart changes how a neighborhood feels in summer. Tree canopies block direct solar heat on asphalt, while soil beds soak up sudden downpours that would otherwise flood storm drains.

Social researchers have noticed equally important human effects. Large destination parks require a planned weekend trip for elderly residents or parents with toddlers, whereas a bench beneath zelkova trees fifty meters from a grocery store invites spontaneous ten-minute rests every day. Regular eye contact among neighbors watering flower beds also builds informal community trust.

Maintaining thirty scattered mini-parks can stretch municipal gardening crews thin if handled centrally. Successful cities solve this by pairing public tree pruning with neighborhood "park friends" volunteers who sweep leaves, plant seasonal bulbs, and report broken lights.

Grand city parks remain irreplaceable treasures, yet weaving tiny green pockets into everyday streets proves that nature does not have to be huge to transform urban life.

examples.script:
A Museum You Can Hear

At the Riverside Museum, most visitors once followed signs from one glass case to another. They read short descriptions of old tools, clothes, and furniture, then moved on. The objects were interesting, but the museum staff noticed that many visitors did not stay long. Few people understood how the objects had been used in daily life.

To change this, the museum invited local residents to record stories about familiar objects. One woman described the sound of the sewing machine her mother used at home. A retired baker explained why a wooden tray had a particular shape. These recordings were added to a small audio player that visitors could borrow at the entrance. The aim was not to replace the written descriptions but to provide another way to explore the collection.

The first recordings were long and difficult to follow. Staff had assumed that visitors would listen to complete interviews. In practice, people wanted to move at their own speed. The museum therefore divided the interviews into short sections. Each section focused on one object and lasted less than two minutes. Visitors could choose only the stories that interested them.

The new system also changed the relationship between the museum and the town. Residents who had rarely visited came to hear their relatives' recordings. Some brought photographs or offered to share their own memories. The museum checked these stories against old records before using them, because personal memories are not always exact.

A visitor survey later showed that people were spending more time in the museum. However, the director did not regard longer visits as the only sign of success. She was more pleased that visitors were asking new questions about everyday life in the past. The museum now plans to add stories from younger residents as well. The staff believe that objects which seem ordinary today may help future visitors understand the present.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第9回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
Why Old Bridges Were Built with Roofs

Travel through rural valleys in Switzerland, Austria, North America, or parts of Japan, and you may cross a wooden bridge that looks remarkably like a long narrow barn floating above a river. Tourists often assume the roof and side walls were added so travelers and horses could stay dry during sudden storms—or so nervous farm animals would not fear the rushing water below.

While shelter was a pleasant bonus, carpenters of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries had a much more practical structural reason: protecting the heavy timber trusses underneath from rot. An uncovered wooden bridge exposed to rain, snow, and summer sun typically needed major replacement within fifteen to twenty years. Water seeped into joints where beams met, froze and expanded in winter, and invited wood-eating fungi.

Adding a lightweight roof and shingle siding cost extra lumber at the start, yet shielded the load-bearing beams from moisture. When minor roof shingles wore out, villagers could replace them cheaply without closing the bridge or rebuilding its main frame. Protected this way, many covered timber bridges lasted eighty to over a hundred years—four or five times longer than open wooden spans.

When affordable steel and reinforced concrete arrived in the twentieth century, engineers no longer needed roofs to weatherproof bridges. Nevertheless, communities that preserved historic covered bridges have gained unexpected value: calm pedestrian crossings, local landmarks, and living lessons in resource-saving craftsmanship.

Sometimes the smartest way to make a structure endure is not choosing a rarer material, but keeping everyday weather off its bones.

examples.script:
How Hospital Gardens Speed Patient Recovery

Throughout much of the mid-twentieth century, modern hospital architecture prioritized sterile efficiency above all else. Landscaped courtyards that once surrounded nineteenth-century infirmaries were paved over for parking decks and diagnostic wings, leaving patient rooms facing blank brick walls or air-conditioning shafts.

A turning point arrived in 1984 when environmental psychologist Roger Ulrich examined ten years of surgical recovery charts at a suburban Pennsylvania hospital. Patients recovering from identical gallbladder operations had been assigned randomly to rooms along one corridor: half looked out on a small stand of deciduous trees, while the other half faced a plain brown brick wall. Patients with the tree view requested significantly fewer strong painkillers, reported lower anxiety to nurses, and went home nearly a full day sooner on average.

Follow-up clinical studies in Japan, Sweden, and the United States confirmed that visual and physical contact with greenery lowers stress hormones such as cortisol and steadies heart rate—not only in patients, but also among exhausted ICU nurses and family caregivers taking ten-minute breaks.

Today, architects design "healing gardens" onto hospital rooftops and inner courtyards with careful medical input. Smooth, glare-free paths accommodate wheelchairs and IV poles safely; fragrant herbs and seasonal blossoms help stroke patients rebuild sensory orientation, while toxic or heavy-pollen plants are excluded near allergy wards.

Greenery cannot replace skilled surgeons or antibiotics, of course, yet restoring nature to hospital grounds treats the human nervous system alongside the illness.

The quiet label

A small theatre once put a "quiet performance" label on certain shows. Staff expected it to welcome people who disliked sudden noise. However, a visitor explained that the label was unclear: did it mean the audience had to remain completely silent, or that the sound from the stage would be softer? The theatre asked several visitors to review its website. It then replaced the short label with a description of what would be different. These performances now use lower sound levels and leave a few lights on. Visitors may step outside and return. The theatre still offers ordinary performances, but it no longer expects a single label to explain every change.

Why Libraries Lend Sewing Machines and Tools

For generations, people thought of public libraries solely as quiet halls lined with books, magazines, and newspapers. Over the past decade, however, dozens of municipal libraries have added an unexpected shelf near the checkout counter—one stocked with sewing machines, pruning shears, air-quality monitors, and cake pans.

The idea behind a "library of things" is straightforward. Many household tools are genuinely useful twice a year, yet sit gathering dust in a closet for the other fifty weeks. Buying a decent sewing machine just to hem two pairs of curtains is expensive, especially for students or young families living in compact apartments with little storage space. Borrowing equipment with an ordinary library card lets residents (21).

Sharing infrequent tools brings community benefits as well. Librarians often pair popular items with beginner workshops led by retired tailors or carpenters, turning solitary repairs into friendly learning sessions. In this way, lending practical tools extends a library's traditional mission: giving everyone equal access to (22) regardless of income.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第1回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
A Museum You Can Hear

At the Riverside Museum, most visitors once followed signs from one glass case to another. They read short descriptions of old tools, clothes, and furniture, then moved on. The objects were interesting, but the museum staff noticed that many visitors did not stay long. Few people understood how the objects had been used in daily life.

To change this, the museum invited local residents to record stories about familiar objects. One woman described the sound of the sewing machine her mother used at home. A retired baker explained why a wooden tray had a particular shape. These recordings were added to a small audio player that visitors could borrow at the entrance. The aim was not to replace the written descriptions but to provide another way to explore the collection.

The first recordings were long and difficult to follow. Staff had assumed that visitors would listen to complete interviews. In practice, people wanted to move at their own speed. The museum therefore divided the interviews into short sections. Each section focused on one object and lasted less than two minutes. Visitors could choose only the stories that interested them.

The new system also changed the relationship between the museum and the town. Residents who had rarely visited came to hear their relatives' recordings. Some brought photographs or offered to share their own memories. The museum checked these stories against old records before using them, because personal memories are not always exact.

A visitor survey later showed that people were spending more time in the museum. However, the director did not regard longer visits as the only sign of success. She was more pleased that visitors were asking new questions about everyday life in the past. The museum now plans to add stories from younger residents as well. The staff believe that objects which seem ordinary today may help future visitors understand the present.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第6回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
How Curved Sidewalk Corners Shape Street Safety

Most pedestrians never think twice about the shape of a street corner where two sidewalks meet. Yet traffic engineers know that the radius of that curve—whether it forms a sharp ninety-degree turn or a wide, sweeping arc—has a direct effect on how fast cars turn and how safely people cross.

During the mid-twentieth century, many cities widened intersection corners into gentle curves so large trucks and buses could turn without slowing down much. While convenient for vehicles, wide curves had two drawbacks for walkers. First, drivers could swing around corners at twenty-five or thirty kilometers per hour while looking mainly for oncoming cars rather than people in the crosswalk. Second, rounding off the corner pushed the curb back, making the painted crosswalk several meters longer for children and older residents to cross.

In recent years, urban planners have been tightening residential and school-zone corners again. A tighter curb forces passenger cars to slow to walking pace before turning, giving drivers an extra second or two to spot someone stepping off the sidewalk. Extending the corner slightly—a design often called a "curb bulb"—also shortens the crossing distance and lets pedestrians see past parked cars without stepping into traffic.

What about fire engines and delivery trucks that still need room to turn? Engineers solve this in creative ways. On some corners, they build a low, textured stone apron beside the curb: ordinary cars stay off the bumpy surface, while the wide wheels of an emergency vehicle can roll slowly over it when necessary.

Small geometric changes in concrete rarely make headlines, yet reshaping a single corner can calm an entire neighborhood crossing every day of the year.

examples.script:
Why Coastal Towns Paint Lighthouses in Distinct Stripes

Postcards of seacoasts often show a tall white lighthouse standing on a rocky headland. Travel along an actual coastline, however, and you quickly notice that neighboring lighthouses rarely look identical: one wears bold red-and-white horizontal bands, another spirals like a black-and-white barber pole, and a third is painted solid yellow.

At night, sailors identify lighthouses by their unique flash rhythm—for instance, two quick flashes every ten seconds. During daylight hours, however, a flashing lamp is hard to spot against bright sky or sea glare. Before satellite navigation existed, captains steering along a foggy coast with binoculars needed an unmistakable visual daytime marker, known to mariners as a "daymark." Giving adjacent towers contrasting patterns ensured that (21).

Background scenery also guides color choice. A pure white tower stands out sharply against dark pine forests, yet vanishes against chalk cliffs or winter snowdrifts, where red bands remain vivid. Even today, when ships carry digital chart plotters, maritime authorities maintain these painted daymarks as (22) whenever electronics fail at sea.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問3 長文の語句空所補充｜第10回（問21〜22）
examples.script:
Why Bakeries Slash Bread Dough Before Baking

Look closely at a crusty French baguette or country loaf, and you will notice diagonal cuts running neatly across the golden top. Home bakers often assume these slashes—known professionally as "scoring"—are merely a baker's artistic signature. While distinct patterns do help identify different loaves, a sharp blade actually solves a basic physics problem inside a hot oven.

The moment raw dough hits a hot baking stone, yeast activity surges and trapped water turns into steam, causing the loaf to puff up rapidly during the first ten minutes. Meanwhile, dry oven heat quickly hardens the outer skin into a firm crust. If no cuts have been made, expanding gas pushes against the weakest random spot on the side or bottom, tearing an uneven blowout and leaving the interior dense in one half and hollow in the other. Scoring creates deliberate expansion joints so the loaf (21).

Angle and depth matter too. Holding the blade nearly flat creates a thin flap of dough that peels back into a crisp, caramelized ridge prized for flavor. Thus, a two-second cut just before baking controls both (22).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第14回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
How Botanical Gardens Use Wood Libraries

When visitors stroll through a botanical garden or natural history museum, pressed leaves and dried blossoms in herbarium cabinets usually come to mind as plant collections. Tucked away in climate-controlled basements from Kew Gardens in London to Kyoto and Madison, Wisconsin, however, researchers curate a lesser-known archive that looks like a carpenter's dream bookshelf: thousands of polished rectangular blocks of wood shelved spine-out like hardcover novels, known as a "xylarium."

Carved from documented trees collected around the globe over the past two centuries, each block records a species' unique cellular architecture. Slice a sliver of wood thinner than tissue paper and place it under a microscope, and its water-conducting vessels, rays, and growth rings form a fingerprint as distinctive as human DNA—even decades after a tree was felled and turned into furniture or flooring.

That anatomical library now plays a frontline role against illegal logging, one of the world's most destructive wildlife crimes. Rare tropical rosewoods, mahoganies, and ebonies protected by international treaties look nearly identical to legal plantation timber once sawn into smooth planks and stacked inside shipping containers. Customs officers at ports used to rely on paper export certificates that smugglers easily forged.

By training portable machine-vision cameras and chemical spectrometers on verified xylarium blocks, wood anatomists have given border inspectors field tools that identify protected tree species on the dock within minutes.

Old museum blocks have helped art historians and luthiers too—dating medieval oak panels and matching repair wood for historic bridges—proving that carefully cataloged specimens gain unexpected value long after they are collected.
