examples.script:
Why Public Clocks Still Matter in the Smartphone Era

Almost everyone walking through a train station plaza or town square today carries an exact atomic-synced clock in a coat pocket. At first glance, spending municipal money to maintain large analog clocks on towers, schools, and park posts might seem outdated. Yet when cities remove broken public clocks instead of repairing them, residents surprisingly often petition to bring them back.

One reason is practical convenience in moments when hands are occupied. A parent holding a toddler's hand, a cyclist waiting at an intersection, or a commuter carrying grocery bags in winter gloves can check a clock face in half a second without unzipping a pocket. Even more importantly, pulling out a smartphone just to check the time frequently leads to unintended distraction—one glance at a notification banner, and five minutes vanish.

Urban designers point to a subtler social role as well. Unlike a private screen, a public clock creates a shared reference point in physical space. Saying "Let's meet under the station clock at two" gives friends and visitors an unmistakable landmark visible from across a crowded square. During major power or cellular outages following storms, wind-up or battery-backed tower clocks have also continued marking time calmly when digital displays went dark.

Maintaining outdoor clocks does require skilled hands. Gears exposed to freezing rain, sea breeze, and nesting birds must be cleaned and lubricated regularly, and fewer young technicians train in turret clockwork today. To keep costs manageable, some towns pair modern solar-charged movements behind historic dial faces, preserving the familiar look while simplifying upkeep.

Far from being mere nostalgia, a well-placed town clock quietly supports punctual, unhurried movement through shared streets.

Each team will have ninety minutes to bake twelve identical rolls or pastries featuring at least one fruit or vegetable grown in our prefecture. All dry ingredients must be weighed in the hall after the start signal; bringing pre-mixed dough from home is against the rules. However, fruit compotes or roasted sweet-potato fillings that require long simmering may be prepared the day before and brought in a sealed cooler box.

Because six teams share four large convection ovens, oven slots are staggered every ten minutes. Your team's assigned baking window is printed on the badge you will receive at 9:30 a.m. check-in.

Good luck to all bakers!
Contest Secretariat

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第10回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
How Pocket Parks Cool Busy Neighborhoods

When city governments talk about expanding green space, residents often picture sprawling central parks with boating ponds and long jogging loops. Finding ten empty hectares inside an already crowded district, however, is nearly impossible. Instead, urban planners from Tokyo to Madrid are turning tiny leftover plots—a vacant corner lot, a former gas station, or two unused parking spaces—into "pocket parks."

Measuring smaller than a tennis court, a single pocket park may hold just four shade trees, a permeable brick path, a drinking fountain, and three wooden benches. Modest as that sounds, grouping dozens of small green oases a five-minute walk apart changes how a neighborhood feels in summer. Tree canopies block direct solar heat on asphalt, while soil beds soak up sudden downpours that would otherwise flood storm drains.

Social researchers have noticed equally important human effects. Large destination parks require a planned weekend trip for elderly residents or parents with toddlers, whereas a bench beneath zelkova trees fifty meters from a grocery store invites spontaneous ten-minute rests every day. Regular eye contact among neighbors watering flower beds also builds informal community trust.

Maintaining thirty scattered mini-parks can stretch municipal gardening crews thin if handled centrally. Successful cities solve this by pairing public tree pruning with neighborhood "park friends" volunteers who sweep leaves, plant seasonal bulbs, and report broken lights.

Grand city parks remain irreplaceable treasures, yet weaving tiny green pockets into everyday streets proves that nature does not have to be huge to transform urban life.

examples.script:
How Quiet Floors Help Hospital Patients Recover

When patients stay overnight in a hospital, uninterrupted sleep is one of the strongest aids to healing. Ironically, hospital wards have long been among the hardest places to sleep soundly. Alongside necessary medical monitors, everyday corridor sounds—squeaking supply carts, echoing footsteps on hard vinyl tiles, and clicking door latches—repeatedly wake light sleepers.

Acoustic researchers measuring ward noise found that sudden peaks in sound disturb sleep far more than a low, steady hum. A metal cart rolling over a tiny seam in a hard floor can send a sharp sixty-five-decibel clatter into nearby rooms, raising a sleeping patient's heart rate even if the person does not fully remember waking up.

To tackle this problem without sacrificing hygiene, hospital designers have rethought flooring and hardware from the ground up. New rubber-composite floors cushion footsteps and cart wheels while remaining seamless and easy to disinfect—unlike carpets, which trap dust and spills. Equally simple mechanical changes help: replacing metal trash-can lids with slow-closing dampers and fitting supply carts with soft polyurethane casters cut corridor noise spikes nearly in half during pilot studies.

Staff well-being improves alongside patient rest. Nurses walking ten kilometers per shift on cushioned rubber floors report less knee and back fatigue, and quieter hallways reduce misunderstandings when doctors discuss medication doses.

Thoughtful hospital design recognizes that recovery depends not only on advanced medicine, but also on a calm sensory environment.

The objects were interesting, but the museum staff noticed that many visitors did not stay long. Few people understood how the objects had been used in daily life.

To change this, the museum invited local residents to record stories about familiar objects. One woman described the sound of the sewing machine her mother used at home. A retired baker explained why a wooden tray had a particular shape. These recordings were added to a small audio player that visitors could borrow at the entrance. The aim was not to replace the written descriptions but to provide another way to explore the collection.

The first recordings were long and difficult to follow. Staff had assumed that visitors would listen to complete interviews. In practice, people wanted to move at their own speed. The museum therefore divided the interviews into short sections. Each section focused on one object and lasted less than two minutes. Visitors could choose only the stories that interested them.

The new system also changed the relationship between the museum and the town. Residents who had rarely visited came to hear their relatives' recordings. Some brought photographs or offered to share their own memories. The museum checked these stories against old records before using them, because personal memories are not always exact.

A visitor survey later showed that people were spending more time in the museum. However, the director did not regard longer visits as the only sign of success. She was more pleased that visitors were asking new questions about everyday life in the past. The museum now plans to add stories from younger residents as well. The staff believe that objects which seem ordinary today may help future visitors understand the present.

examples.script:
Why Old Roof Tiles Get a Second Job

Walk through an older Japanese town after a renovation project, and you may see stacks of dark gray clay roof tiles waiting beside a garden wall. Historically, clay tiles were prized because they protected wooden houses from heavy rain and summer heat for decades. Yet when old houses are replaced with modern buildings, thousands of still-solid tiles are removed every year. Disposing of them in landfills takes up space and wastes durable material.

In several regions, landscape designers and town workers have found practical ways to reuse discarded tiles without melting them down. Crushed into small pieces, the baked clay absorbs rainwater and releases it slowly, making it an ideal surface for park paths and tree beds. Unlike dark asphalt, crushed tile paths stay cooler under strong summer sun and allow weeds to be pulled out easily.

Whole tiles are useful as well. Placed upright in rows half-buried in soil, their gentle curves form neat borders around vegetable patches and flower beds. Some community gardens even stack tiles with narrow gaps between them to create cool shelters for frogs and helpful insects that eat garden pests.

Reusing tiles is not completely effortless. Workers must first remove nails, mortar, and cracked pieces with sharp edges so that paths and borders are safe to walk near. Even with this extra sorting step, local towns have found that cleaning and crushing old tiles nearby requires far less energy than manufacturing new concrete blocks and transporting them from distant factories.

For many residents, the greatest benefit is visual as well as environmental. Seeing familiar gray tiles along a new park walkway preserves a quiet connection to the town's past, turning construction waste into part of the neighborhood's character.

examples.script:
How Quiet Floors Help Hospital Patients Recover

When patients stay overnight in a hospital, uninterrupted sleep is one of the strongest aids to healing. Ironically, hospital wards have long been among the hardest places to sleep soundly. Alongside necessary medical monitors, everyday corridor sounds—squeaking supply carts, echoing footsteps on hard vinyl tiles, and clicking door latches—repeatedly wake light sleepers.

Acoustic researchers measuring ward noise found that sudden peaks in sound disturb sleep far more than a low, steady hum. A metal cart rolling over a tiny seam in a hard floor can send a sharp sixty-five-decibel clatter into nearby rooms, raising a sleeping patient's heart rate even if the person does not fully remember waking up.

To tackle this problem without sacrificing hygiene, hospital designers have rethought flooring and hardware from the ground up. New rubber-composite floors cushion footsteps and cart wheels while remaining seamless and easy to disinfect—unlike carpets, which trap dust and spills. Equally simple mechanical changes help: replacing metal trash-can lids with slow-closing dampers and fitting supply carts with soft polyurethane casters cut corridor noise spikes nearly in half during pilot studies.

Staff well-being improves alongside patient rest. Nurses walking ten kilometers per shift on cushioned rubber floors report less knee and back fatigue, and quieter hallways reduce misunderstandings when doctors discuss medication doses.

Thoughtful hospital design recognizes that recovery depends not only on advanced medicine, but also on a calm sensory environment.

examples.script:
Audio Descriptions at Live Theater

Going to see a live play is exciting partly because so much happens without words: an actor glances nervously at a clock, a door slowly opens at the back of the stage, or warm yellow light shifts to cold blue. For theatergoers who are blind or have low vision, however, these silent visual moments can make a story hard to follow if they rely on dialogue alone.

To bridge this gap, more theaters now offer "audio-described" performances. Audience members who request the service wear a lightweight earpiece connected to a small receiver. Sitting in a soundproof booth at the back of the hall, a trained describer watches the stage and speaks quietly into a microphone, slipping short phrases about costumes, facial expressions, and movements into the natural pauses between actors' lines.

Writing good audio description is more delicate than simply listing everything on stage. If a mystery character hides a key in a coat pocket, naming the key too early could spoil a surprise that sighted audience members discover only later. Conversely, saying too little leaves listeners confused when everyone else gasps or laughs. Describers therefore attend rehearsals in advance, consult directors, and time every sentence down to the second.

Some theaters have also introduced "touch tours" thirty minutes before the curtain rises. Visitors who use audio description are invited onto the stage to feel the texture of a velvet cape, examine a wooden prop sword, and walk across the set to understand the distance between rooms. When the play begins, a brief phrase like "she crosses to the oak table" immediately calls up a clear mental picture.

Actors and directors say preparing for these performances often sharpens their own craft as well. Explaining why a gesture or lighting change matters forces the creative team to think carefully about every visual choice on stage.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第4回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
Teaching Buses and Trains to Wait Two Minutes

Missing a rural connecting bus by ninety seconds can turn a twenty-minute commute into an hour-long wait on a windy platform. In large cities, where another train arrives every four minutes, tight transfers rarely matter. Along regional rail lines and suburban bus corridors, however, vehicles run far less frequently, so a single delayed train can strand dozens of passengers who needed that connection.

Historically, bus drivers had no reliable way to know whether an approaching train was running two minutes late or twenty. Waiting blindly risked making every downstream stop late and causing passengers further along the route to miss their own appointments. As a result, most operators instructed drivers to depart strictly by the printed clock, even if a train was just pulling into the station.

Low-cost GPS trackers and shared dispatch screens have begun changing this rigid rule. In several mid-sized European and Japanese cities, trains and connecting buses now exchange live location updates automatically. If a train is delayed by three minutes or less—and the bus schedule has enough cushion on a quiet stretch of road to make up that time—the screen on the driver's dashboard flashes a "hold" request. Meanwhile, an announcement inside the train tells transferring riders that their bus is waiting at Stand 2, preventing dangerous sprinting on station stairs.

Of course, holding a bus is not always wise. When heavy snow delays a train by fifteen minutes, holding every feeder bus would paralyze the entire local network. Dispatch software therefore sets clear upper limits, typically three to five minutes, and prioritizes the last evening runs when no later bus exists.

Passenger surveys in towns using smart-hold rules show a notable jump in trust toward public transit. Knowing that operators coordinate across vehicles makes people far more willing to leave their cars at home for two-seat journeys.

examples.script:
Borrowing Umbrellas That Actually Come Back

Many train stations keep a basket of free umbrellas near the exit for commuters caught in sudden rain. The idea is generous, yet most stations face the same problem: within a few weeks, the basket is empty. People rarely steal the umbrellas on purpose; instead, once the sky clears, they simply forget to bring them back.

Two years ago, a commuter railway tried a small experiment at five stations. Rather than buying plain black umbrellas, it partnered with a local high school art club. Students painted bright patterns—such as river fish, autumn leaves, and yellow trains—on the handles and panels. Each umbrella also carried a short tag saying which station was waiting for it to "come home." Surprisingly, this design helped (21).

Over six months, more than eighty percent of the painted umbrellas were returned, compared with fewer than thirty percent before. Commuters said an umbrella with a hand-painted tag felt like a borrowed item from a neighbor rather than a disposable object. For the students, seeing their artwork travel through town on rainy evenings became (22). Several other stations have since asked schools along their lines to join the project.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問3 長文の語句空所補充｜第4回（問21〜22）
examples.script:
Why Bakery Windows Fog Up Less Than Before

On cold winter mornings, small bakeries face a practical display problem. Warm steam rising from fresh trays of bread meets the icy glass of the front window and turns into tiny water droplets. While a misty window looks cozy in picture books, shop owners dislike it when passersby cannot see which breads have just come out of the oven.

Turning up the heater near the glass dries the window, yet dry hot air also makes uncovered croissants and crusty loaves lose moisture faster. A baker in Matsumoto found a simpler fix after talking with a neighbor who repaired eyeglasses. By installing a quiet ceiling fan that kept air moving gently across the glass and leaving a two-centimeter vent open near the top frame, the shop prevented warm damp air from sitting still against the cold pane. This adjustment (21) without drying out the bread.

Keeping the window clear had a welcome effect on morning sales. Commuters walking to the station could spot steaming walnut rolls from across the street and step inside on impulse. Sometimes solving an everyday shop problem requires (22) rather than buying a bigger heater.

Please arrive at the back door to help move supplies.

Second, the local bus company cannot provide the extra morning service we requested. Some visitors may arrive later than planned. We will therefore begin serving food at 11:30 instead of 11:00. Volunteers should still arrive at 9:00, as originally arranged. We need that time to set up the tables and check the kitchen equipment.

If you are helping at a food table, please bring a clean apron. We will provide gloves and name tags. Volunteers at the information desk do not need aprons. Those who have not yet chosen a job should contact me by Thursday evening.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第6回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
How Curved Sidewalk Corners Shape Street Safety

Most pedestrians never think twice about the shape of a street corner where two sidewalks meet. Yet traffic engineers know that the radius of that curve—whether it forms a sharp ninety-degree turn or a wide, sweeping arc—has a direct effect on how fast cars turn and how safely people cross.

During the mid-twentieth century, many cities widened intersection corners into gentle curves so large trucks and buses could turn without slowing down much. While convenient for vehicles, wide curves had two drawbacks for walkers. First, drivers could swing around corners at twenty-five or thirty kilometers per hour while looking mainly for oncoming cars rather than people in the crosswalk. Second, rounding off the corner pushed the curb back, making the painted crosswalk several meters longer for children and older residents to cross.

In recent years, urban planners have been tightening residential and school-zone corners again. A tighter curb forces passenger cars to slow to walking pace before turning, giving drivers an extra second or two to spot someone stepping off the sidewalk. Extending the corner slightly—a design often called a "curb bulb"—also shortens the crossing distance and lets pedestrians see past parked cars without stepping into traffic.

What about fire engines and delivery trucks that still need room to turn? Engineers solve this in creative ways. On some corners, they build a low, textured stone apron beside the curb: ordinary cars stay off the bumpy surface, while the wide wheels of an emergency vehicle can roll slowly over it when necessary.

Small geometric changes in concrete rarely make headlines, yet reshaping a single corner can calm an entire neighborhood crossing every day of the year.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 大問4 読解｜第12回（問23〜29）
examples.script:
Why Botanical Illustrators Still Draw Plants by Hand

Modern smartphones and macro cameras can photograph an orchid petal in a fraction of a second, capturing millions of pixels of color. Given such effortless technology, visitors to natural history museums are often surprised to learn that botanists naming a newly discovered plant species still commission black-and-white pen-and-ink illustrations drawn by hand.

A single photograph, however sharp, shows only one individual plant at one moment in time. In the wild, a flower may bloom in April while its seed pod matures in August, or one leaf may be chewed by insects while a diagnostic root tuber stays hidden underground. Even worse, camera lenses struggle with depth of field at close range: focusing sharply on tiny pollen stamens blurs the stem hairs two centimeters behind them.

A trained botanical illustrator overcomes all of these limits on one sheet of paper. Consulting closely with the botanist—and often examining pressed herbarium specimens under a microscope—the artist combines buds, open blossoms, cross-sections of fruit, and magnified seed textures side by side in crystal-clear focus. Unnecessary shadows and distracting background leaves are omitted so another scientist a century later can verify the exact vein pattern that distinguishes the species from close relatives.

Digital tablets have certainly joined traditional crow-quill pens on many illustrators' desks, making revisions cleaner. Yet the core skill remains human observation rather than button-pressing: deciding which tiny details matter scientifically.

Far from competing, photography and hand illustration complement each other—photos record living color in habitat, while botanical line art preserves clear structural truth.

examples.script:
Why Escalators Have Brushes Along Their Sides

Look down at the bottom edges of almost any subway or department-store escalator, and you will notice rows of stiff black nylon bristles sticking inward from both side panels. Many riders casually use them to dust off their shoes—or assume the brushes are there to sweep candy wrappers off the moving steps. In fact, engineers added skirt brushes after investigating a serious mechanical hazard.

Between each moving metal step and the stationary side wall sits a tiny gap just a few millimeters wide. Without a physical barrier, soft rubber rain boots, trailing coat drawstrings, or long shopping bags resting right against the wall can get pulled into that gap by friction as the steps descend. Once fabric or rubber wedges inside, the escalator must halt abruptly. (18), a subtle sensory warning was needed to keep feet a few centimeters toward the center.

Stiff nylon bristles solve the problem gently through human reflexes. Whenever a passenger's shoe or pant leg brushes against the bristles, the light tickling sensation prompts the person to shift inward automatically without looking down. (19), the bristles physically deflect loose shoelaces before they can reach the narrow metal clearance.

Safety authorities made side brushes mandatory on new escalators in many countries after injury rates dropped sharply in early trials. Sometimes the best engineering safeguard is not a loud alarm, but (20).

examples.script:
Keeping Track of City Trees

On a summer afternoon, a tree-lined street can feel quite different from a nearby road without shade. Trees also provide places for birds and insects to live. Yet city officials often have incomplete information about the trees they are responsible for. Paper records may be old, and different departments may keep separate lists. This can make it difficult to decide where care is most urgently needed.

In one city, a group of residents offered to help create a shared tree record. Volunteers walked along public streets and entered basic information into a mobile form. They recorded each tree's location, took a photograph, and noted visible signs of damage. They were not asked to judge whether a tree was safe. That decision remained the responsibility of trained specialists.

The first month produced thousands of entries, but some were unreliable. A tree near a street corner might be recorded by two teams, while a photograph taken from far away might show the wrong tree. Rather than simply count the entries, the project leader introduced a checking stage. Teams compared neighboring records, and specialists reviewed reports of possible disease. Each confirmed tree received a single identification number.

The resulting map changed how the city planned its work. Officials had previously responded mainly to requests from residents. However, some neighborhoods made many requests while others made few, even when their trees were in poor condition. The new record allowed officials to compare areas more fairly. It also revealed streets where there were very few trees at all.

The project did not mean that every neighborhood could immediately receive new trees. Planting requires money, and there must be enough space underground for roots as well as above ground for branches. In some streets, water pipes and cables limited the available space. Officials had to explain why a request could not always be accepted.

For volunteers, the main lesson was that collecting information was only the beginning. The value of the record depended on checking it, keeping it current, and using it to answer practical questions. The group now revisits a different area each month. Its members hope that a record built through public participation will remain useful because people understand both its purpose and its limits.

How Bamboo Scaffolding Still Rises Around High-Rise Towers

Visitors stepping onto the streets of Hong Kong for the first time often look up in disbelief: encasing forty-story glass skyscrapers are intricate lattices of golden bamboo poles lashed together with black nylon strips. In an era of steel cranes and aluminum frames, traditional bamboo scaffolding remains a thriving engineering craft.

Speed, weight, and flexibility explain bamboo's staying power in dense subtropical cities. Thick giant-timber bamboo stalks weigh a fraction as much as steel pipes yet boast remarkable tensile strength along their hollow fibers. Experienced scaffolders carry bundles easily up narrow stairwells and tie custom grids around irregular balconies or curved neon signs without welding or heavy bolts. (21), a skilled crew can wrap a mid-rise facade far faster and at lower cost than with rigid metal tubing.

Typhoon winds reveal another surprising advantage. Whereas rigid steel frames can transmit violent gusts into building anchors or snap suddenly, properly braced bamboo flexes slightly with the wind to absorb energy. Safety standards are far from casual, however: Hong Kong building codes specify pole thickness, curing age, steel wall-anchors, and formal apprenticeships. (22), many modern projects use a hybrid approach—steel brackets at the base supporting bamboo lattices above.

Combining renewable fast-growing grass with rigorous safety engineering shows that traditional materials can (23).

examples.script:
Why Escalators Leave One Side Debate Behind

In many busy subway stations, commuters follow an unwritten rule on escalators: stand on one side and leave the other lane clear for people in a hurry. At first glance, this arrangement seems polite and efficient. In recent years, however, transit operators from Tokyo to London have begun asking riders to stand in both lanes and refrain from walking on moving steps.

Safety was the initial concern. Escalator steps are much taller than ordinary stairs, so a single misstep by someone carrying a bag can cause a chain of falls. Yet engineers studying station crowds found a second, surprising problem. When ninety percent of riders prefer to stand, reserving half the escalator for the few who walk leaves the walking lane mostly empty. (18), queues at the bottom grow longer during rush hour.

Field trials confirmed the math. Stations that guided commuters to stand two abreast moved roughly twenty-five percent more people per minute than stations using the stand-and-walk split. Standing evenly also reduced uneven mechanical wear on rollers and chains, because (19).

Changing habits formed over decades takes patience, of course. Clear floor footprints and calm voice reminders work better than scolding posters, helping riders understand that (20).

examples.script:
A New Plan for the Exhibition

From: Elena Brooks, Project Leader
To: Student Exhibition Team
Subject: Final arrangements

Dear team,
Thank you for preparing the exhibition on the history of our neighborhood. After looking through your work, the community center has agreed to lend us its main hall. This will allow us to display larger photographs than we could in the school corridor. However, the hall is available for only one weekend, so we must finish setting up by Friday evening and remove everything on Sunday after closing.

We originally planned to borrow display boards from the town office. Unfortunately, they are needed for another event. The center has offered lightweight stands instead. examples.script:
Saving Seeds in School Gardens

Many elementary and junior high schools plant cherry tomatoes or sunflowers each spring using packets of commercial seeds. Students water the beds, harvest the crop in summer, and clear the plot in autumn. The next April, teachers buy fresh seed packets and repeat the cycle. While children learn how plants grow, they seldom see how one generation of plants produces the next.

A group of science teachers in Nagano decided to extend this lesson by teaching students to collect and store seeds from their own harvest. The task turned out to require more care than simply drying a few pods on a windowsill. If seeds were sealed in jars while still slightly damp, mold ruined them over winter. Students had to measure weight changes over several days to confirm that the seeds were dry enough. (21), the project connected biology with careful data recording.

The teachers also noticed an unexpected change in how students treated the garden in late summer. Plants that had finished fruiting were once pulled up right away because they looked untidy. Once students understood that seed pods needed weeks on the stem to ripen fully, they put up small explanatory signs rather than clearing the beds prematurely. Visitors learned that the brown stalks were (22).

Not every saved seed sprouted the following spring, and cross-pollination occasionally produced surprising shapes in pumpkins. Far from being failures, these variations sparked lively classroom questions about genetics. Passing labeled envelopes of seeds to the incoming grade gave students (23).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 大問2 長文の語句空所補充｜第15回（問18〜23）
examples.script:
How Repair Cafés Extend Product Lifespans and Neighborhood Ties

Buy an electric toaster, desk fan, or winter coat today, and a single snapped switch or stuck zipper often sends the entire item to the trash bin. Manufacturers frequently seal plastic housings with glue rather than screws, while commercial repair shops must charge labor fees that rival the price of a cheap replacement. Across more than two thousand towns worldwide—having started in Amsterdam in 2009—community volunteers have built a welcoming response: the monthly "Repair Café."

Held in libraries, church basements, or civic centers on Saturday afternoons, a Repair Café pairs retired engineers, tailors, carpenters, and tech-savvy students with neighbors carrying broken household goods. Visitors pay nothing except optional donations for spare fuses or thread. Crucially, the café is not a drop-off counter; owners pull up a chair and hold the flashlight or screwdriver alongside the fixer. (21), demystifying how a coffee maker or bicycle brake works gives people confidence to tackle minor upkeep at home.

Volunteer groups log every attempted repair in a shared international database, successfully reviving roughly two-thirds of items brought in. Beyond keeping tons of metals and textiles out of landfills, those records now inform "right-to-repair" lawmakers pressing appliance makers to supply spare parts and screw-together designs. (22), elderly craftspeople living alone gain a lively monthly venue where younger neighbors genuinely value their decades of practical skill.

Sharing tools over a cup of tea shows how local grassroots action can (23).

examples.script:
Borrowing time

A city library introduced appointments for help with digital devices. Each appointment lasted twenty minutes. Staff could keep to the schedule easily when a visitor had one simple question. However, some visitors needed to explain a longer series of problems before staff understood the situation. Extending every appointment would have reduced the number of people the library could serve. Instead, the library added a short conversation at the booking stage. Staff now ask what the visitor hopes to do, rather than only which device they own. They can then choose a standard slot or arrange a longer session. The system is not perfect: some problems still take longer than expected. Nevertheless, fewer sessions now end before the main difficulty has even been identified.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 大問3 読解｜第2回（問24〜31）
examples.script:
Repair Cafes and How Products Are Designed

Across many cities, weekend "repair cafes" invite residents to bring broken toasters, lamps, and bicycles to community halls where skilled volunteers help fix them for free. Most visitors come with a practical goal: extending the life of a household item and keeping it out of the trash. Over the past decade, however, these grassroots gatherings have begun producing something else of value—detailed records of why everyday appliances fail.

Volunteers at dozens of repair groups log each item's brand, approximate age, and the specific fault they encountered. When thousands of entries are combined, clear patterns emerge. For example, a handheld vacuum might have a motor capable of running for ten years, yet be discarded after two because a tiny plastic latch on the dust cup snaps and no spare part is sold. Similarly, some kettles cannot be opened without breaking glued seams, making even a simple switch repair nearly impossible.

Consumer advocacy groups and engineering schools have started using this shared data in constructive ways. Design instructors assign students to examine broken appliances from repair logs and redesign weak joints or sealed casings so they can be unscrewed with standard household tools. Meanwhile, policy discussions in several countries now reference repair-cafe statistics when proposing rules that require manufacturers to supply basic replacement parts for a set number of years.

Manufacturers sometimes argue that sealed, lightweight designs keep production costs low and protect users from tampering with dangerous electrical components. Safety is a legitimate concern, especially with high-voltage devices. For that reason, repair advocates distinguish between parts that ordinary owners can safely swap—such as filters, batteries, and latches—and internal components that should only be serviced by certified technicians.

Ultimately, the data gathered at neighborhood tables shows that durability is shaped long before an item breaks. While volunteers can rescue individual machines one Saturday at a time, lasting waste reduction depends on feeding those hands-on lessons back into how products are engineered in the first place.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 大問3 読解｜第9回（問24〜31）
examples.script:
How Seed Vaults Keep Crop Diversity Alive Underground

Walk through a modern supermarket, and the fruit and vegetable section looks wonderfully varied. Yet agricultural historians point out a quiet vulnerability behind that colorful display: globally, just nine plant species account for nearly two-thirds of all crop production, and farmers within each crop increasingly plant a handful of high-yielding commercial varieties. While uniform crops simplify harvesting and transport, genetic uniformity carries risk. If a new fungal disease or prolonged drought strikes a widely planted wheat or potato variety, entire regions can lose harvests simultaneously.

Over previous centuries, peasant farmers maintained thousands of local "landrace" varieties—grains and beans adapted to salty coastal soil, high mountain frost, or short desert rains. When farms switch to modern commercial seeds, those hardy older varieties can vanish within a single generation unless someone preserves viable seeds.

That is the mission of over a thousand seed banks worldwide, backed up by the Svalbard Global Seed Vault deep inside an Arctic mountain in Norway. Sealed in moisture-proof foil packets at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, orthodox seeds such as wheat, rice, and lentils slow their metabolism so dramatically that they remain capable of sprouting for decades or even centuries. Permafrost surrounding the Arctic rock tunnel provides natural refrigeration even if external power temporarily fails.

Even the coldest vault is not a "set-and-forget" museum, however. Seeds slowly lose vigor over time and must periodically be thawed, planted in soil, harvested fresh, and frozen anew. Moreover, tropical crops with moist, fleshy seeds—such as cacao, mango, and avocado—cannot survive standard freezing at all; scientists preserve their diversity in living field collections or ultra-cold liquid nitrogen.

Safeguarding ancient seeds is ultimately forward-looking work: traits hidden in an obscure mountain grain today may hold the exact drought resistance breeders need fifty years from now.

Instructions for the Saturday Wetland Bird Count

From: M. Kurata, Bird Conservation Group
To: Student Survey Volunteers
Subject: Observation points and quiet-zone rules for Saturday

Dear student volunteers,
Thank you for joining our winter waterfowl count at Ashihara Marsh this Saturday morning. Migratory ducks and wild geese feed near the reed beds soon after sunrise, so we will meet at the south parking shelter at 6:40 a.m. and walk to our four wooden hides in small groups.

Each group includes an experienced spotter with a high-powered scope; your job is to record species counts every fifteen minutes on the waterproof clipboards provided. Please switch your phones to silent mode and turn screen brightness all the way down before entering a hide, as sudden flashes of white light through the viewing slots can startle resting flocks.

Because two hides stand over shallow water, icy breezes come up through the floorboards. Wear wool socks—two thin pairs trap more warmth than one tight thick pair—and bring a thermos of warm drink if you like, though strongly scented soup should wait until we return to the shelter at 9:30 a.m.

Best regards,
M. Kurata

examples.script:
Why Cities Are Uncovering Buried Streams

Beneath the asphalt of almost every major city flow dozens of forgotten brooks and small rivers. During periods of rapid urban growth in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, engineers routinely encased neighborhood streams in underground concrete pipes—known as culverts—to gain flat land for roads, prevent rubbish dumping, and move rainwater out of town as fast as possible. Out of sight, these waterways vanished from maps and local memory alike.

Climate pressures and aging pipes are now prompting municipalities to reverse course through a practice called "daylighting"—lifting buried streams back into open air. Ironically, the old concrete channels designed to prevent localized puddles often worsen flooding downstream during intense modern cloudbursts. Smooth underground pipes shoot storm runoff forward all at once, overwhelming river junctions below. An open channel lined with stones, curves, and terraced banks slows the water down and gives high flows safe room to spread.

Bringing water back to the surface transforms urban neighborhoods in quieter months as well. Shaded streamside paths run several degrees cooler than surrounding streets on August afternoons, while riffles oxygenate the water enough for dragonflies, minnows, and herons to return within a remarkably short time. Shopkeepers along famous daylighting projects—from Seoul to Zurich—have seen foot traffic rise as once-noisy traffic lanes become pleasant places to linger.

Daylighting is not feasible everywhere, of course. Where apartment blocks or subway tunnels sit directly atop a culvert, rerouting the stream through an adjacent park strip or widening parallel greenways may be the only practical option, and upstream street runoff must be filtered through gravel beds before entering the open brook.

Even modest stretches of uncovered water remind residents that a city is built atop living geography rather than a blank concrete slab.

examples.script:
Borrowing More Than Books

A small library wanted to attract residents who rarely borrowed books. Instead of expanding its shelves, it began lending useful household objects, including a sewing machine and a set of gardening tools. The staff hoped that residents could try an object before deciding whether to buy one. People could also borrow items they needed only occasionally.

At first, the library accepted almost every donated object. This created an unexpected problem. Some items were missing parts, while others required repairs that the staff could not perform. The service soon became difficult to manage. The library therefore introduced a rule: every object had to be inspected before it was accepted. (18), donations became easier to handle, even though the library received fewer of them.

Another concern was that borrowers might return objects late. The library considered charging large fines, but staff worried this would discourage people from trying the service. Instead, borrowers received a reminder a day before an item was due. If they needed more time, they could request an extension unless someone else was waiting. The library found that clear communication was (19).

The service is still small. Staff have not claimed that it will replace shopping or solve all the town's waste problems. However, residents have started discussing which objects could usefully be shared. For the library, one important result has been (20). People who had never met now exchange advice about using and repairing the objects they borrow.

examples.script:
Why Escalators Leave One Side Debate Behind

In many busy subway stations, commuters follow an unwritten rule on escalators: stand on one side and leave the other lane clear for people in a hurry. At first glance, this arrangement seems polite and efficient. In recent years, however, transit operators from Tokyo to London have begun asking riders to stand in both lanes and refrain from walking on moving steps.

Safety was the initial concern. Escalator steps are much taller than ordinary stairs, so a single misstep by someone carrying a bag can cause a chain of falls. Yet engineers studying station crowds found a second, surprising problem. When ninety percent of riders prefer to stand, reserving half the escalator for the few who walk leaves the walking lane mostly empty. (18), queues at the bottom grow longer during rush hour.

Field trials confirmed the math. Stations that guided commuters to stand two abreast moved roughly twenty-five percent more people per minute than stations using the stand-and-walk split. Standing evenly also reduced uneven mechanical wear on rollers and chains, because (19).

Changing habits formed over decades takes patience, of course. Clear floor footprints and calm voice reminders work better than scolding posters, helping riders understand that (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 大問2 長文の語句空所補充｜第12回（問18〜23）
examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Pack Berries in Vented Clamshell Boxes

Pick up a container of strawberries, raspberries, or blueberries at the market, and you will almost always find them sitting in a clear hinged plastic box perforated with narrow slots along the lid and base. Shoppers sometimes wish berries came in sealed airtight tubs or simple paper bags, yet post-harvest food scientists designed those slotted "clamshell" boxes around how delicate fruit breathes.

Even after leaving the vine, fresh berries remain living tissue: they consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide, heat, and water vapor. Seal warm berries inside an airtight container, and moisture condenses on the lid within an hour, creating damp droplets where gray mold spores multiply overnight. Conversely, loose paper bags crush soft raspberries during truck transport and hide bruised fruit at the bottom. Slotted clamshells cushion berries against bumps while letting cold refrigerator air flow straight through the stack. (18), berries reach home kitchens days fresher with far less spoilage.

Packaging waste is a real concern, of course. Because sticky label glue once ruined recycling batches, many producers now stamp product codes directly onto 100% recycled PET lids or test molded-pulp baskets with breathable cellulose windows. (19), shoppers should resist washing berries until right before eating—rinsing them days early traps water between seeds and speeds decay.

Balancing protective airflow with cleaner materials helps farmers and households alike (20).

examples.script:
How Ice Stupas Store Winter Water for Spring Crops

High in the cold desert valleys of Ladakh in northern India, farmers receive less than ten centimeters of rain a year. For centuries, villages depended on summer meltwater trickling down from mountain glaciers to irrigate barley, peas, and apricot trees. As smaller low-altitude glaciers have retreated, however, streams now run dry during critical planting weeks in April and May, only to surge later in July.

Building concrete reservoirs at four thousand meters is costly, and shallow ponds freeze solid or evaporate quickly in fierce high-altitude sun. In 2013, local engineer Sonam Wangchuk tested an ingenious geometric alternative: piping unused winter stream water downhill by gravity and spraying it upward into subzero night air. Freezing as it falls, the spray builds a towering cone of ice thirty meters tall, shaped like a traditional Buddhist monument or stupa. (21), a cone exposes far less surface area to spring sunshine per liter of ice than a flat pond does.

Because of that compact shape, an ice stupa melts slowly throughout April, May, and June—releasing steady trickles of water right when young barley shoots need moisture most. How Hospital Courtyards Support Recovery

For much of the late twentieth century, hospital architecture prioritized compact efficiency: air-conditioned towers with short walking distances for staff, wipe-clean corridors, and sealed windows. Courtyards and gardens, once common around older infirmaries, were often paved over for parking or extra diagnostic wings. Over the past twenty years, however, medical planners have been bringing greenery back into the heart of hospital buildings—not merely as decoration, but as a practical aid to care.

Interest grew after clinical studies compared patients recovering from similar surgeries in rooms facing trees with those facing blank brick walls. Patients with a view of foliage tended to report less discomfort, sleep more steadily, and transition home slightly sooner. Subsequent research in rehabilitation wards showed that accessible outdoor courtyards motivated patients learning to walk again: reaching a sunlit bench beside seasonal flowers felt like a meaningful goal compared with counting tiles down a fluorescent hallway.

Designing an effective hospital garden requires far more care than planting a public park. Paths must be wide, level, and glare-free so IV poles and wheelchairs roll without jolting. Strongly scented lilies or heavy pollen-producing trees can bother patients sensitive to smells after chemotherapy, so landscape architects favor gentle textures, rustling bamboo, trickling water, and herbs whose fragrance appears only when someone chooses to brush a leaf. Shaded seating pockets also give family members and nurses a quiet five-minute refuge to reset emotionally between difficult conversations.

Skeptics understandably ask whether garden maintenance belongs in tight healthcare budgets. Yet hospitals that track staff turnover and visitor satisfaction increasingly treat well-designed courtyards as shared infrastructure. When nurses have a calm place to step outside on break and patients move more willingly during physical therapy, modest landscaping pays quiet returns across the whole institution.

How Wildlife Overpasses Reconnect Divided Forests

On highway maps, a new four-lane expressway cutting across a mountain range looks like a thin ribbon just thirty meters wide. To deer, bears, badgers, and forest tortoises living on either side, however, unfenced high-speed traffic—or twin rows of tall crash fencing—acts like an impassable concrete canyon. Wildlife biologists studying roads over the past forty years found that slicing one large forest into isolated patches does far more harm than roadkill collisions alone.

Cut off from neighboring valleys, small animal populations lose access to seasonal food—such as low-valley oak acorns in autumn—and begin inbreeding within a few generations, weakening genetic resistance to disease. Early highway engineers tried installing narrow concrete drainage pipes beneath roads, assuming animals would crawl through them. While foxes and raccoons adapted quickly to dark tunnels, cautious grazing mammals such as elk and deer refused to enter cramped spaces where predators might ambush them.

Canada's Banff National Park pioneered a bolder answer in the 1990s along the Trans-Canada Highway: wide, soil-covered "wildlife overpasses" fifty meters broad, planted with native shrubs, pine trees, and log piles so the bridge looks and smells like a continuous forest clearing from an animal's eye level. Low earth berms along the sides block headlight glare and tire roar from trucks passing underneath.

Motion-triggered infrared cameras across Banff's six overpasses and thirty-eight underpasses have recorded more than two hundred thousand safe crossings by grizzlies, wolves, moose, and lynx, slashing large-mammal vehicle collisions by over eighty percent—a major win for human driver safety and auto insurers as well.

Today, countries from the Netherlands and Germany to Japan and the United States build green bridges into new road budgets from the start, proving that transport networks and wildlife corridors can share the same landscape.

Why Supermarkets Adjust Their Music

Shoppers rarely pay conscious attention to the music playing overhead while they push a cart down an aisle. Yet retail researchers have long studied how tempo and volume subtly shape behavior inside stores. Fast, energetic songs tend to make people walk more briskly, whereas slower instrumental tracks encourage customers to pause and examine shelves.

A regional grocery chain recently reconsidered its daytime playlist after receiving feedback from older residents and parents of young children. Many found the combination of bright lights, announcements, and upbeat pop songs exhausting. In response, the chain introduced "quiet mornings" twice a week, turning off promotional broadcasts and lowering music volume. (18), complaints dropped and weekday morning visits grew steadily.

Interestingly, staff members benefited just as much as shoppers. Cashiers and shelf stockers spend up to eight hours in the store, hearing the same loop of songs repeatedly. When the store switched to calmer, varied acoustic pieces during regular hours, employees reported feeling less fatigued at the end of a shift. This mattered because (19).

The chain did not eliminate lively music altogether; weekend afternoon sales events still feature brighter playlists. However, managers stopped treating background sound as mere filler. They learned that (20) can make an ordinary errand noticeably less stressful for everyone inside the building.

How Ferries Cut Fuel Use with Wind Rotor Sails

When people picture wind-powered ships, they usually imagine canvas sails billowing from wooden masts. Modern car ferries and cargo vessels look nothing like nineteenth-century clippers, yet a growing number now carry tall, spinning white cylinders on their decks to capture wind energy alongside regular engines.

These cylinders, known as rotor sails, rely on a physical principle familiar to baseball pitchers and tennis players. When a motor spins the vertical cylinder slowly in a crosswind, air speeds up on one side of the drum and slows down on the other. The resulting pressure difference pushes the ship forward at right angles to the wind. Because the motor spinning the cylinder uses only a tiny fraction of the thrust generated, ferries crossing windy straits can throttle back their main diesel engines. (21), operators on North Sea routes have recorded fuel savings of eight to fifteen percent.

Unlike fabric sails, rotor cylinders require no extra deck crew to hoist or fold when squalls hit; bridge computers adjust rotation speed automatically as wind direction changes. (22), some designs tilt flat onto the deck at the push of a button so the ship can pass safely beneath low harbor bridges.

Rotor sails cannot power a heavy ferry on calm days, nor are they meant to work alone. Rather, combining aerodynamic physics with modern automation gives shipping lines (23) while cleaner fuels are still scaling up.

How Ice Stupas Store Winter Water for Spring Crops

High in the cold desert valleys of Ladakh in northern India, farmers receive less than ten centimeters of rain a year. For centuries, villages depended on summer meltwater trickling down from mountain glaciers to irrigate barley, peas, and apricot trees. As smaller low-altitude glaciers have retreated, however, streams now run dry during critical planting weeks in April and May, only to surge later in July.

Building concrete reservoirs at four thousand meters is costly, and shallow ponds freeze solid or evaporate quickly in fierce high-altitude sun. In 2013, local engineer Sonam Wangchuk tested an ingenious geometric alternative: piping unused winter stream water downhill by gravity and spraying it upward into subzero night air. Freezing as it falls, the spray builds a towering cone of ice thirty meters tall, shaped like a traditional Buddhist monument or stupa. (21), a cone exposes far less surface area to spring sunshine per liter of ice than a flat pond does.

Because of that compact shape, an ice stupa melts slowly throughout April, May, and June—releasing steady trickles of water right when young barley shoots need moisture most. Local youths maintain the pipes without electric pumps, since height difference alone creates water pressure. (22), villages can store millions of liters of winter runoff using simple hardware-store pipes.

Ice stupas cannot replace glacier conservation on a global scale, yet they give mountain communities (23) while adapting to shifting snowmelt seasons.

examples.script:
Why Traditional Terraced Rice Fields Matter Beyond Harvests

Carved step by step into steep hillsides across Japan, the Philippines, southern China, and Indonesia, stone-and-earth terraced paddies—known in Japanese as tanada—look like shimmering mirrors in May and golden staircases in September. Built by hand over centuries where flat valley land was scarce, many mountain terraces now face abandonment because narrow, curved plots cannot accommodate large ride-on harvesters and aging farming populations find steep stone walls exhausting to maintain.

Judged strictly by tons of rice produced per hour of labor, tiny hillside paddies can never compete with vast laser-leveled plains. Yet hydrologists and municipal planners downstream have begun calculating the hidden public services those stepped fields perform every rainy season. Thousands of low earth bunds act collectively like a staircase of miniature check dams: instead of hurtling down bare slopes in destructive mudslides, typhoon rain pauses briefly in paddy after paddy, filtering slowly into mountain aquifers that feed clear village springs all winter.

Biodiversity thrives in that mosaic of shallow water and stone walls too. Rare frogs, dragonflies, and aquatic beetles that vanished from concrete-lined lowland canals depend on warm, pesticide-light terrace pools to breed, while wild herbs cling to dry stone risers.

Keeping terraces alive requires sharing the burden beyond individual farm households. Across Japan, "tanada ownership" programs invite city families to pay a modest annual fee and join four seasonal weekends—planting seedlings, weeding, harvesting by hand, and sharing freshly steamed rice with veteran farmers. Elsewhere, chefs pay premium prices for mineral-rich mountain-spring rice, and rural towns train young volunteers in dry-stone wall repair.

Preserving terraced hillsides is not mere nostalgia; it sustains living green infrastructure that protects valleys and culture together.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 大問3 読解｜第15回（問24〜31）
examples.script:
How Roman Aqueducts Moved Water by Gravity Alone

Postcard photos of ancient Roman engineering almost always feature soaring multi-tiered stone arches—like the Pont du Gard in southern France or the Aqueduct of Segovia in Spain—striding dramatically across sunlit river valleys. Looking at those monumental bridges, casual travelers often assume Roman aqueducts ran entirely above ground on stone stilts. In reality, arches made up less than ten percent of most aqueduct routes; the other ninety percent wound invisibly through stone-lined channels buried half a meter to several meters underground.

Keeping channels underground made practical sense: buried conduits stayed cool, resisted evaporation, kept dirt and grazing animals out of drinking water, and required far less quarried stone than tall arches. What made Roman hydraulic engineering extraordinary was that the entire fifty- or eighty-kilometer journey from mountain spring to city fountain relied solely on gravity, without a single mechanical pump.

Surveyors had to maintain an almost imperceptibly gentle downward slope—often dropping just fifteen to thirty centimeters per kilometer, or less than the thickness of a textbook over the length of a soccer field. Too steep a gradient turned flowing water into a scouring torrent that eroded mortar walls; too flat a channel let stagnant pools deposit silt.

Without spirit levels or laser sights, Roman engineers used a wooden T-shaped instrument called a chorobates: a six-meter beam fitted with plumb bobs on its legs and a shallow water trough carved along its top to judge true horizontal even on windy hillsides. Where a deep valley blocked the path, arches carried the channel level across; where a ridge intervened, miners chiseled straight tunnels guided by vertical air shafts.

Delivering millions of liters daily to public baths, street fountains, and workshops, gravity-fed aqueducts sustained urban populations rarely matched again in Europe until the nineteenth century.

Why Recipes Sometimes Fail at High Altitude

Travelers staying in a mountain cabin two thousand meters above sea level are often puzzled when a familiar family recipe turns out strangely. Spaghetti takes longer to soften in boiling water, while a sponge cake that rises beautifully near the coast may puff up too fast in the oven and then collapse in the middle.

The cause is lower atmospheric pressure. At sea level, the weight of the air above pushes down on a pot of water, keeping molecules in liquid form until the temperature reaches 100 degrees Celsius. High in the mountains, thinner air exerts less pressure, so water begins boiling at around 93 degrees. Turning up the stove flame only produces more steam; it cannot make the boiling water any hotter. (21), foods cooked by boiling simply need extra minutes to finish.

Baking involves the same physics in reverse. Bubbles of steam and gas inside cake batter expand more forcefully when external air pressure is weak. Before the flour and eggs have time to set into a firm structure, the batter stretches too thin and sinks. Experienced mountain bakers compensate by reducing leavening powder slightly and raising oven temperature a little so the structure firms up sooner. (22), adding a spoonful of extra liquid prevents the batter from drying out in thin, dry mountain air.

Understanding these adjustments turns kitchen frustration into a practical science lesson. A recipe written in a coastal city assumes invisible environmental conditions. Once cooks recognize (23), they can adapt their methods confidently wherever they travel.

How Bamboo Scaffolding Still Rises Around High-Rise Towers

Visitors stepping onto the streets of Hong Kong for the first time often look up in disbelief: encasing forty-story glass skyscrapers are intricate lattices of golden bamboo poles lashed together with black nylon strips. In an era of steel cranes and aluminum frames, traditional bamboo scaffolding remains a thriving engineering craft.

Speed, weight, and flexibility explain bamboo's staying power in dense subtropical cities. Thick giant-timber bamboo stalks weigh a fraction as much as steel pipes yet boast remarkable tensile strength along their hollow fibers. Experienced scaffolders carry bundles easily up narrow stairwells and tie custom grids around irregular balconies or curved neon signs without welding or heavy bolts. (21), a skilled crew can wrap a mid-rise facade far faster and at lower cost than with rigid metal tubing.

Typhoon winds reveal another surprising advantage. Whereas rigid steel frames can transmit violent gusts into building anchors or snap suddenly, properly braced bamboo flexes slightly with the wind to absorb energy. Safety standards are far from casual, however: Hong Kong building codes specify pole thickness, curing age, steel wall-anchors, and formal apprenticeships. (22), many modern projects use a hybrid approach—steel brackets at the base supporting bamboo lattices above.

Combining renewable fast-growing grass with rigorous safety engineering shows that traditional materials can (23).

examples.script:
Why Coin Edges Have Tiny Vertical Ridges

Run your fingernail around the rim of a hundred-yen or fifty-yen coin—or an American quarter or dime—and you feel dozens of crisp vertical grooves, whereas ten-yen and five-yen coins feel completely smooth. Cashiers and vending-machine engineers appreciate that texture today, yet "reeded edges" were invented more than three centuries ago to stop a widespread financial crime.

In seventeenth-century Europe, high-value coins were struck from pure silver or gold whose metal was worth exactly the face value stamped on the coin. Dishonest traders took advantage of soft precious metals by "clipping"—shaving tiny slivers of silver off the irregular edges of hundreds of coins before spending them at full value and melting the scraps into bullion bars. Over time, clipped coins grew noticeably smaller and lighter, undermining trust in everyday commerce. (18), Britain's Royal Mint—guided in the 1690s by warden Isaac Newton—introduced collar dies that stamped uniform grooves around every silver and gold coin's circumference.

With milled ridges in place, shaving even half a millimeter off a coin's rim immediately erased the grooves and exposed the tampering at a glance. Modern coins use cupronickel alloys rather than pure silver, so clipping for bullion is long gone. (19), reeded edges remain invaluable because they let blind and visually impaired shoppers distinguish denominations instantly by touch inside a purse.

Tiny ridges around a coin show how an anti-counterfeiting fix evolved into (20).

Why Mapmakers Deliberately Straightened Subway Lines

Early transit maps of major cities in the 1910s and 1920s tried faithfully to show every twist of a railway line atop an accurate street map. As networks expanded, however, the results became nearly unreadable. Central business districts were crammed with tiny overlapping station names, while long suburban branches stretched off the edges of pocket folders.

In 1931, an electrical engineering draftsman named Harry Beck noticed something crucial while sketching London's Underground during a layoff. Once passengers descend beneath the pavement, they cannot see curving streets or rivers anyway; what they really need to know is which line to board, how many stops remain, and where two lines intersect. Drawing inspiration from electrical circuit diagrams—where wires are arranged neatly at horizontal, vertical, and forty-five-degree angles regardless of physical length—Beck compressed distant suburbs and enlarged the crowded center.

Transit managers initially rejected Beck's draft as too radical, fearing riders would misjudge walking distances on the surface. When the Underground printed a small trial run in 1933, however, commuters embraced its clarity immediately. Within decades, Tokyo, Paris, New York, and Sydney adopted similar schematic diagrams.

The trade-off managers worried about never completely vanished, though. Tourists consulting a schematic subway diagram sometimes take two train transfers to travel between stations that sit just four hundred meters apart above ground. To bridge this gap, several modern transit apps and station boards now blend both worlds—keeping clean geometric lines while adding dotted ten-minute walking arcs or subtle river contours.

Beck's insight remains a classic lesson in information design: leaving out geographic detail that does not serve the user's immediate task can make complex systems far easier to navigate.

How Seed Vaults Keep Crop Diversity Alive Underground

Walk through a modern supermarket, and the fruit and vegetable section looks wonderfully varied. Yet agricultural historians point out a quiet vulnerability behind that colorful display: globally, just nine plant species account for nearly two-thirds of all crop production, and farmers within each crop increasingly plant a handful of high-yielding commercial varieties. While uniform crops simplify harvesting and transport, genetic uniformity carries risk. If a new fungal disease or prolonged drought strikes a widely planted wheat or potato variety, entire regions can lose harvests simultaneously.

Over previous centuries, peasant farmers maintained thousands of local "landrace" varieties—grains and beans adapted to salty coastal soil, high mountain frost, or short desert rains. When farms switch to modern commercial seeds, those hardy older varieties can vanish within a single generation unless someone preserves viable seeds.

That is the mission of over a thousand seed banks worldwide, backed up by the Svalbard Global Seed Vault deep inside an Arctic mountain in Norway. Sealed in moisture-proof foil packets at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, orthodox seeds such as wheat, rice, and lentils slow their metabolism so dramatically that they remain capable of sprouting for decades or even centuries. Permafrost surrounding the Arctic rock tunnel provides natural refrigeration even if external power temporarily fails.

Even the coldest vault is not a "set-and-forget" museum, however. Seeds slowly lose vigor over time and must periodically be thawed, planted in soil, harvested fresh, and frozen anew. Moreover, tropical crops with moist, fleshy seeds—such as cacao, mango, and avocado—cannot survive standard freezing at all; scientists preserve their diversity in living field collections or ultra-cold liquid nitrogen.

Safeguarding ancient seeds is ultimately forward-looking work: traits hidden in an obscure mountain grain today may hold the exact drought resistance breeders need fifty years from now.

examples.script:
Instructions for Participating in the River Salmon Fry Release

From: Kitagawa Watershed Conservation Association
To: Registered Families and High School Volunteers
Subject: Bucket acclimatization rule for Sunday's salmon fry release

Dear participants,
Thank you for joining our annual chum salmon fry release at Kitagawa River Park this Sunday at 10:00 a.m.! Over the winter, student volunteers tended fertilized eggs in chilled hatchery trays, and twelve thousand five-centimeter young salmon are now ready to begin their journey to the Pacific.

When you receive your small plastic bucket of fry at the riverside tent, please do NOT pour the fish straight into the river right away. Hatchery tank water is nine degrees Celsius, whereas sunlit river shallows may be three degrees warmer or cooler; a sudden temperature shock stuns tiny fish and leaves them vulnerable to birds.

Instead, crouch safely at the gravel edge, dip half your bucket into the river to mix river water in gradually over two minutes, and then tilt the rim gently underwater so the fry swim out on their own. Life jackets will be lent to all children under twelve.

Kitagawa Conservation Staff

examples.script:
Guidelines for Borrowing Roof-Snow Measurement Kits

From: Kitano Town Winter Safety Division
To: Neighborhood Association Snow Wardens
Subject: Calibrating borrowed snow-core tubes before December patrols

Dear Snow Wardens,
Thank you for volunteering to monitor roof-snow loads on elderly residents' homes this winter. Measuring snow depth with a ruler alone can be dangerously misleading: forty centimeters of fluffy January powder weighs far less than forty centimeters of rain-soaked February pack, which can quietly overload older timber rafters.

Starting Monday, each district warden may pick up a lightweight aluminum snow-core tube and hanging spring scale at Town Hall Annex Room 104. Push the hollow tube straight down to the roof eaves marker, lift out a vertical cylinder of snow, and weigh it on the hook scale to read water-equivalent load in kilograms per square meter.

Before every morning patrol, hang the empty dry tube on the scale and turn the top brass ring until the pointer reads exactly zero; trapped ice inside the barrel will inflate readings. Please log figures on the shared tablet form by noon.

Winter Safety Division

examples.script:
Designing Hospital Signs Under Stress

Designing directional signs for an airport or mall is challenging, yet hospitals present an even stricter test. Visitors arriving for urgent appointments are often anxious, tired, or unfamiliar with medical terms. A sign pointing to "Otolaryngology" may be technically exact while leaving an elderly patient standing helplessly in the lobby.

When a regional medical center renovated its main building, planners shadowed first-time visitors from the bus stop to exam rooms. People rarely read long wall directories from top to bottom; instead, they looked for one simple cue at each junction. Pairing formal department names with everyday terms—such as "Ear, Nose & Throat"—immediately reduced hesitation. (18), colored stripes along the baseboard reassured visitors that they were still on the right path.

Testing also revealed a placement flaw. Designers had hung overhead panels near the ceiling, yet people pushing wheelchairs or strollers looked straight ahead and walked right under them. Lowering markers to eye level on corner pillars solved the problem. (19), consistent icons—such as a teacup for the cafeteria and a mortar for the pharmacy—helped residents still learning the local language.

Arriving without getting lost lowered visitors' stress before they met a doctor, proving that (20).

Trial of the Flexible Workspace

From: Priya Shah, Facilities Manager
To: Staff in the West Building
Subject: Four-week workspace trial

Dear colleagues,
From next Monday, the third-floor meeting room will be used as a quiet workspace during the morning. This is a four-week trial, not a permanent change. Staff feedback has shown that some tasks require longer periods without interruption than our open office currently allows. The room will remain available for meetings after 1 p.m.

You may reserve a desk through the internal booking page up to two working days ahead. To give more people a chance to participate, please book no more than two mornings per week. If you no longer need a booking, cancel it promptly. Desks cannot be reserved by leaving personal belongings overnight.

During the trial, the room is intended for individual work. Please take telephone and video calls elsewhere, even if you use headphones. There will be no charge to your department for using the room. However, this does not include printing costs, which will continue to be charged in the usual way.

We will record how often desks are used, but the number of bookings will not be our only measure of success. At the end of the trial, participants and their team leaders will be asked whether the arrangement helped them complete suitable tasks and whether it created difficulties for their teams. We also want to hear from staff who wanted to participate but could not find a suitable time.

Please do not assume that the booking rules will remain unchanged after the trial. They will be reviewed along with the room's future use. Send any urgent concerns directly to me rather than waiting for the final survey.

Priya

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 大問3 読解｜第10回（問24〜31）
examples.script:
Why Museums Control Light Exposure with Strict "Lux Budgets"

Step from a sunlit sculpture court into a gallery displaying Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints, medieval illuminated manuscripts, or nineteenth-century watercolor landscapes, and the room can feel surprisingly dim—almost like twilight. Visitors occasionally wonder whether the museum is cutting electricity costs. Conservators have a far more urgent motive: light itself is an invisible chemical force that permanently fades organic pigments and weakens paper fibers.

Unlike oil paintings on canvas or glazed ceramics—whose mineral pigments locked in linseed oil or glass tolerate moderate museum lighting well—plant dyes, insect inks, silk threads, and watercolor washes contain fragile molecular bonds. Photons of light, especially high-energy ultraviolet rays and blue wavelengths, snap those bonds one by one. Worse still, photochemical damage is strictly cumulative and irreversible: exposing a delicate Hiroshige print to bright gallery lamps for one week causes roughly the same fading as ten weeks under lamps one-tenth as bright, and no rest in a dark vault afterward can bring lost blues or purples back.

To balance public enjoyment today against preservation for centuries ahead, major museums manage fragile works under an annual "lux-hour budget." Illuminance is capped at just fifty lux—roughly a fifth of normal office brightness—with all ultraviolet filtered out. Curators also track how many hours each print spends on display; once a work reaches its yearly allowance, say three months, it returns to dark climate-controlled storage while a companion print takes its place.

Modern LEDs free of ultraviolet heat, paired with motion sensors or velvet curtains that visitors lift briefly inside display cases, stretch those precious light budgets further than ever.

Dim rooms and rotating exhibitions may test a visitor's patience, yet they ensure our grandchildren will still see the artist's original colors rather than pale ghosts.
